accuracy-stability.title: A-stability, L-stability and error norms
accuracy-stability.html:
A-stability, L-stability and error norms

A-stability and L-stability describe the response of a time integrator to linear decay modes. L1, L2 and L∞ instead describe the size and distribution of an error. They answer different questions. A method can be stable with a large error, and a small algebraic residual need not imply a small PDE error.

A/L-stability classification and accurate wave amplitudes and speeds are separate questions. For reading the magnitude and argument of an amplification factor, see von Neumann analysis: dissipation and dispersion basics.

A-stability concerns the whole left half-plane#

Apply a one-step method to y′=λy, with z=λΔt. Its stability function satisfies

yn+1=R(z)yn,S={z∈C:∣R(z)∣≤1}. y_{n+1}=R(z)y_n,\qquad \mathcal S=\{z\in\mathbb C:|R(z)|\leq1\}. yn+1​=R(z)yn​,S={z∈C:∣R(z)∣≤1}.

The method is A-stable if its absolute-stability region contains the entire closed left half-plane. In particular, R must have no pole there. Thus a scalar mode with Re λ≤0 does not grow for any positive step size in this test. Dahlquist (1963) is a foundational A-stability reference in the linear-multistep setting. The one-step notation here is used to make the comparison transparent.

Forward Euler, R(z)=1+z, is stable on the negative real axis only for −2≤z≤0. No consistent explicit RK method is A-stable: its nonconstant stability polynomial is unbounded along the negative real axis. Being implicit alone does not guarantee A-stability.

L-stability also damps infinitely stiff modes#

An L-stable one-step method is A-stable and satisfies

lim⁡∣z∣→∞,  Re⁡z<0R(z)=0. \lim_{|z|\to\infty,\;\operatorname{Re}z<0}R(z)=0. ∣z∣→∞,Rez<0lim​R(z)=0.

This extra property damps modes that are much faster than the chosen step. Backward Euler has R(z)=1/(1−z), so it is both A-stable and L-stable. Crank–Nicolson / the trapezoidal rule has

RCN(z)=1+z/21−z/2,lim⁡z→−∞RCN(z)=−1. R_{CN}(z)=\frac{1+z/2}{1-z/2},\qquad \lim_{z\to-\infty}R_{CN}(z)=-1. RCN​(z)=1−z/21+z/2​,z→−∞lim​RCN​(z)=−1.

It is A-stable but not L-stable: very stiff negative-real modes alternate sign and decay only slowly. Implicit midpoint has the same scalar linear R(z), although its nonlinear update is different from the trapezoidal rule. For z=−1000, backward Euler gives about 0.001 in one step, while CN gives about −0.996; the exact factor is exp(−1000).

For the implemented SDIRK2,

γ=1−1/2,R(z)=1+(1−2γ)z(1−γz)2. \gamma=1-1/\sqrt2,\qquad R(z)=\frac{1+(1-2\gamma)z}{(1-\gamma z)^2}. γ=1−1/2​,R(z)=(1−γz)21+(1−2γ)z​.

Its poles are in the right half-plane, it is A-stable and its large-z limit is zero. This is the L-stable two-stage family associated with Alexander (1977). BDF2 is a two-step method: analyze its characteristic roots and parasitic mode, rather than assigning it an arbitrary single-valued R(z).

These are linear absolute-stability statements. Accuracy, nonlinear contractivity, SSP/TVD inheritance, positivity and boundary stability require their own checks. Eigenvalues alone can also miss transient growth of nonnormal operators. An A-stable time step cannot repair an inconsistent spatial discretization, and L-stability cannot make an underresolved transient accurate.

Continuous L1, L2 and L∞ errors#

For scalar error e(x)=u_h(x)−u_ref(x) on a domain Ω,

∥e∥L1=∫Ω∣e∣ dV,∥e∥L2=(∫Ω∣e∣2 dV)1/2,∥e∥L∞=ess sup⁡x∈Ω∣e(x)∣. \|e\|_{L^1}=\int_\Omega |e|\,dV,\qquad \|e\|_{L^2}=\left(\int_\Omega |e|^2\,dV\right)^{1/2},\qquad \|e\|_{L^\infty}=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in\Omega}|e(x)|. ∥e∥L1​=∫Ω​∣e∣dV,∥e∥L2​=(∫Ω​∣e∣2dV)1/2,∥e∥L∞​=x∈Ωesssup​∣e(x)∣.

L1 measures integrated absolute error. L2 emphasizes larger deviations more strongly. L∞ measures the worst error apart from measure-zero sets. For a continuous error on a compact domain, the essential supremum equals the maximum. For discontinuous solutions, the value assigned exactly at a jump does not change the continuous norm.

For a domain with volume V, mean absolute error is L1/V and RMS error is L2/√V. These normalized quantities have the same physical units as u; unnormalized integral norms also contain powers of length. State the convention before comparing domains of different size.

Discrete weights and the reference representation#

For finite-volume error e_i between a numerical cell mean and a reference cell mean, with positive cell volumes V_i,

E1=∑iVi∣ei∣,E2=(∑iVi∣ei∣2)1/2,E∞=max⁡i∣ei∣. E_1=\sum_iV_i|e_i|,\qquad E_2=\left(\sum_iV_i|e_i|^2\right)^{1/2},\qquad E_\infty=\max_i|e_i|. E1​=i∑​Vi​∣ei​∣,E2​=(i∑​Vi​∣ei​∣2)1/2,E∞​=imax​∣ei​∣.

On a uniform grid, V_i=h^d. On the unit interval, these become mean absolute error, RMS error and maximum cell-mean error. On a nonuniform mesh, an unweighted arithmetic mean generally gives the wrong spatial weighting. For e=(1,3) and cell volumes (0.75,0.25), E1=1.5, E2=√3 and E∞=3; unweighted means disagree.

The Euclidean vector norm np.linalg.norm(e) omits the h^(d/2) factor of a physical discrete L2 norm. Comparing that raw norm across meshes can therefore change an apparent convergence exponent. Relative error E_p/||u_ref||_p needs a stated reference norm; when the denominator is zero, it is undefined. Any regularization must be explicitly reported.

A reference at cell centers is not an exact cell-average reference. DG and FEM need reconstruction and quadrature inside elements; a coefficient-vector norm is not automatically a function L2 norm. Likewise, a maximum over sample points is a sampled L∞ diagnostic, not necessarily the exact supremum of a high-order reconstructed field. Vector components with different units should be reported separately or nondimensionalized with stated scales.

Convergence, shocks and algebraic residuals#

For matched runs at the same physical time and error convention, the observed order is

pobs=log⁡(Ecoarse/Efine)log⁡(hcoarse/hfine). p_{obs}=\frac{\log(E_{coarse}/E_{fine})}{\log(h_{coarse}/h_{fine})}. pobs​=log(hcoarse​/hfine​)log(Ecoarse​/Efine​)​.

Temporal error, reference error, quadrature error, roundoff and incomplete iterative convergence can mask spatial order. Refine time separately, or state how Δt scales with h. Adaptive ODE tolerance is a local, component-scaled error control; it is not a global spatial L2 error bound.

Different norms can behave differently near shocks. For example, an O(1) error supported on width O(h) has L1=O(h), L2=O(√h) and L∞=O(1). This simple scaling is not a universal convergence-rate claim for a shock solver. A useful L1 refinement result need not imply maximum-norm convergence of a shifted jump.

For Ax=b, the residual is r=b−Ax. The solution error satisfies x_num−x_exact=−A^(−1)r, so conditioning matters. An algebraic residual compares against the discrete equation; discretization error compares that equation's solution against the continuous problem. See sparse/nonlinear solvers and the Lax–Richtmyer discussion.

Where the atlas reports each quantity#

  • The equation gallery reports L1/MAE, L2/RMS and L∞ over its stored unit-interval profiles. Its labels retain the distinction between exact cell means, point-sampled Euler references and absent references.
  • The browser stability laboratory has a point-sampled L1/MAE diagnostic and amplification factors; it does not thereby measure a reconstructed finite-volume function norm.
  • P1 FEM integrates L2 and H1 seminorm errors inside triangles.
  • Periodic MAC flow reports a combined velocity RMS error and maximum absolute discrete divergence. These are different diagnostics.
  • Stiff integration reports maximum error over accepted time nodes, separate from nonlinear stage residuals and local step estimates.

Original exhibits keep their documented conventions; this chapter does not retroactively relabel point samples as cell averages or certify a missing maximum-norm calculation.

advanced-limiters.title: Advanced limiters: TVB and positivity preservation
advanced-limiters.html:
Advanced limiters: TVB and positivity preservation

The limiter notebook includes a TVB scalar experiment and a separate conservative Euler-state scaling demonstration. These address different failure modes: loss of accuracy near a smooth extremum and inadmissible thermodynamic states.

TVB modified minmod#

For a candidate increment v and neighboring increments a and b, define

m~(v,a,b)={v,∣v∣≤MΔx2,m(v,a,b),otherwise, \widetilde m(v,a,b)= \begin{cases} v,&|v|\le M\Delta x^2,\\ m(v,a,b),&\text{otherwise}, \end{cases} m(v,a,b)={v,m(v,a,b),​∣v∣≤MΔx2,otherwise,​

where m is the generalized minmod: the smallest magnitude with a shared sign, and zero when signs disagree. Our scalar demonstration chooses v=(a+b)/2. At M=0 this reduces to the two-increment minmod used in the TVD experiment. At M>0 sufficiently small increments survive even when the neighboring slopes have opposite signs, permitting a smooth peak to remain curved.

The dx-squared threshold reflects the scale of smooth-extremum face deviations in the RKDG setting. Its coefficient has units of solution divided by length squared; it is not a universal dimensionless constant. Rescaling the dependent variable or coordinates requires reconsidering M. Increments and derivatives require different thresholds.

Cockburn and Shu (1989) develop the TVB RKDG framework. This edition implements the modified-minmod building block in scalar finite volumes, rather than that full RKDG method or its theorem. The notebook computes M=0,10,50 on both the sine and square pulse. Compare errors and measured maximum TV: allowing small extrema means TV need not decrease at every step, and a large M can also admit small oscillations beside a discontinuity. Changing M does not prove a uniform TVB bound for an arbitrary method. No Euler-system TVB extension is implemented.

Positive density and pressure are different constraints#

For ideal-gas conservative variables U=(rho,m,E),

p(U)=(γ−1)(E−∣m∣22ρ),G={U:ρ>0, p(U)>0}. p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{|m|^2}{2\rho}\right),\qquad \mathcal G=\{U:\rho>0,\ p(U)>0\}. p(U)=(γ−1)(E−2ρ∣m∣2​),G={U:ρ>0, p(U)>0}.

Positive density alone does not ensure positive internal energy. TVD, TVB, an entropy fix, and the absence of visible wiggles do not automatically make Euler states admissible. A negative pressure can arise from excessive kinetic energy even when rho and E are positive.

A mean-preserving scaling building block#

Start with an admissible conservative cell average Ubar. Scale every supplied reconstruction point by the same factor:

U^α=Uˉ+θ(Uα−Uˉ),0≤θ≤1. \widehat U_\alpha=\bar U+\theta(U_\alpha-\bar U),\qquad 0\le\theta\le1. Uα​=Uˉ+θ(Uα​−Uˉ),0≤θ≤1.

If the original points have quadrature mean Ubar, the scaled points retain it. Using a single theta across components and points is essential to this particular construction. Clipping rho, pressure, or total energy independently does not have that conservation property.

First bound theta by the minimum reconstructed density:

θρ=min⁡(1,ρˉ−ϵρρˉ−ρmin⁡)if ρmin⁡<ϵρ;θρ=1 otherwise. \theta_\rho=\min\left(1, \frac{\bar\rho-\epsilon_\rho}{\bar\rho-\rho_{\min}}\right) \quad\text{if }\rho_{\min}<\epsilon_\rho; \qquad\theta_\rho=1\text{ otherwise}. θρ​=min(1,ρˉ​−ρmin​ρˉ​−ϵρ​​)if ρmin​<ϵρ​;θρ​=1 otherwise.

Then shrink theta in [0,theta_rho] until every supplied point also satisfies p(Uhat) ≥ epsilon_p. Ideal-gas pressure is concave for positive density, so the admissible part of this line segment contains the mean and can be found by bisection. The implementation uses 64 iterations and a small roundoff retreat. Density and pressure floors are input parameters, not inserted mass or energy. Inadmissible averages raise an error; scaling around a bad mean cannot repair conservation and positivity together in this way.

This follows the convex-scaling idea of Zhang and Shu (2010), with a deliberately simple common-state scaling and numerical pressure search. It is not a line-by-line reproduction of their two-stage density-polynomial and state limiter. The implementation covers the supplied points only; arbitrary polynomial values between those points are not automatically bounded.

What the demonstration actually verifies#

The three-node cell has xi=-1,0,1, positive Gauss–Lobatto weights (1/6,2/3,1/6), gamma=1.4, and Ubar=(1,0,2.5). The raw states are Ubar + xi times delta. Choose delta=(1.2,0,0) for a density violation, (0,3,0) for a pressure violation, or (1.2,3,1) for a combined violation. Their weighted mean is exactly Ubar in real arithmetic. The plot samples only these three nodes and reports theta, minimum limited density, minimum limited pressure, and the conservative mean defect, with epsilon_rho=epsilon_p=1e-8. These are constructed reconstruction tests, not blast-wave or rarefaction time integrations.

import numpy as np
from numart.limiters import positive_reconstruction

mean = np.array([1., 0., 2.5])
raw = mean + np.array([-1., 0., 1.])[:, None] * [0., 3., 0.]
limited, theta = positive_reconstruction(mean, raw)

Tests check that an already admissible reconstruction is unchanged, bad means are rejected, and both floors and conservative quadrature means survive the three failure cases.

From reconstruction to a fully discrete guarantee#

A complete positivity-preserving Euler method also needs a compatible positivity-preserving numerical flux, positive quadrature decomposition including interface states, a corresponding wave-speed/CFL restriction, and limiting at all required stages. SSP time stepping propagates a forward-Euler positivity property only when that property and its step restriction already hold. Source terms and boundary treatment require their own checks.

This helper is not wired into the existing Euler MUSCL, finite-difference WENO, CT/GLM, or KEEP time updates. Those solvers retain their documented limitations. A future complete implementation should add stage-by-stage admissibility and conservation checks, near-vacuum double rarefaction, and strong blast-wave tests before claiming positivity preservation over time. Multidimensional and non-ideal-EOS extensions need additional analysis.

advanced.title: Preconditioning, dual time stepping, and residual distribution
advanced.html:
Preconditioning, dual time stepping, and residual distribution

Condition numbers and PDE preconditioning#

For Ax=b, the 2-norm condition number is κ₂(A)=σmax/σmin. It measures sensitivity to perturbations rather than the convergence rate of a particular iteration. Left preconditioning gives P^{-1}Ax=P^{-1}b; right preconditioning gives AP^{-1}y=b, x=P^{-1}y. For symmetric positive-definite systems, P^{-1/2}AP^{-1/2} supports symmetry-preserving comparisons.

conditioning_example constructs A=S B S, where B is a 1D Poisson matrix and S is diagonal scaling. It demonstrates the change in condition number under symmetric Jacobi scaling. It does not implement Turkel's low-Mach flow preconditioning matrix.

Compressible PDEs pose a separate preconditioning problem when low-Mach convective and acoustic characteristic speeds differ greatly. A pseudo-time system such as Γ(U) ∂U/∂τ + R(U)=0 modifies characteristic speeds, convergence, and numerical dissipation. Deriving Γ, transforming variables, choosing Mach-dependent coefficients, and maintaining boundary consistency require additional verification. Replacing the physical time derivative indiscriminately changes the time-dependent solution. Turkel (1987).

Dual time stepping#

Applying BDF2 in physical time to dU/dt+R(U)=0 gives

3Un+1−4Un+Un−12Δt+R(Un+1)=0. \frac{3U^{n+1}-4U^n+U^{n-1}}{2\Delta t}+R(U^{n+1})=0. 2Δt3Un+1−4Un+Un−1​+R(Un+1)=0.

At each physical step, evolve the pseudo-time equation for Q,

dQdτ+3Q−4Un+Un−12Δt+R(Q)=0, \frac{dQ}{d\tau}+\frac{3Q-4U^n+U^{n-1}}{2\Delta t}+R(Q)=0, dτdQ​+2Δt3Q−4Un+Un−1​+R(Q)=0,

to a steady state. Backward Euler starts the first step. Physical-time accuracy depends on Δt, spatial error, and incomplete inner convergence. A large physical CFL alone does not establish accurate time evolution. Jameson (1991).

dual_time_advection is a minimal periodic 1D example: implicit upwind advection with BDF1/BDF2, solved by a Jacobi pseudo-time iteration. The inner residual threshold is tol*max(1,||b||∞), with default tol=1e-10. Failure to converge within the iteration limit raises an error. Tests compare against an independent dense solve of the BDF2 discrete equations. This is a reduced model rather than Jameson's complete compressible-flow multigrid algorithm.

Residual distribution schemes#

Distribute an element residual Φ_K=∫K ∇·F(U) dV to its nodes while preserving Σ_{i∈K} Φ_i^K=Φ_K. This conservation condition connects continuous finite elements with upwind ideas. Abgrall (2006), author-hosted review.

rd_residual is a minimal 1D P1 scalar-advection example. It assigns all of Φ_K=a(u_{i+1}-u_i) to the downstream node and divides by lumped mass h. Tests establish equivalence to first-order upwind differences in this case. 2D triangular N/LDA schemes, nonlinear blending, time-consistent mass matrices, and Euler systems remain unimplemented.

Roe, entropy fixes, Einfeldt, and rotated solvers#

Roe uses a linearization satisfying F_R-F_L=Ã(U_R-U_L) and its eigensystem. This edition forms sqrt(ρ)-weighted u and H, with ã²=(γ-1)(H̃-ũ²/2), and adds dissipation through wave strengths and eigenvectors. Roe (1981).

The entropy fix replaces the absolute acoustic eigenvalue below δ with (λ²+δ²)/(2δ). HLLE is a separate flux using Einfeldt-type left/right wave speeds for strong low-density expansions. Roe entropy correction, HLLE positivity properties, and carbuncle treatments address different problems. Einfeldt (1988), Einfeldt et al. (1991).

Rotated-hybrid Riemann solvers combine fluxes using directions beyond the face normal to balance shock robustness and shear-layer resolution. A coordinate rotation alone does not reproduce this construction. This edition adds a specified directional HLLE/Roe composition and cylinder-forebody tests. This explicit two-flux experiment is distinct from an optimized reproduction of the original Rotated-RHLL dissipation formula. Nishikawa–Kitamura (2008).

Roe's Property U#

Roe's 1981 paper, author-uploaded full text, pp. 359–360 uses four conditions: (i) a linear mapping from conserved-state space to flux space for each fixed state pair; (ii) the coincident-state limit equals the physical Jacobian; (iii) the matrix maps the state jump exactly onto the flux jump; (iv) its eigenvectors are linearly independent. The two-state matrix need not depend linearly on its arguments. For physical ideal-gas Euler states the construction below also has real acoustic/contact speeds.

Here is the algebra implemented and independently checked in this atlas. For U=(ρ,ρu,E), H=(E+p)/ρ, set z=√ρ(1,u,H). Then

U(z)=(z12z1z2(z1z3+(γ−1)z22/2)/γ),F(z)=(z1z2((γ+1)z22/2+(γ−1)z1z3)/γz2z3). U(z)=\begin{pmatrix}z_1^2\\z_1z_2\\ (z_1z_3+(\gamma-1)z_2^2/2)/\gamma\end{pmatrix},\qquad F(z)=\begin{pmatrix}z_1z_2\\ ((\gamma+1)z_2^2/2+(\gamma-1)z_1z_3)/\gamma\\z_2z_3\end{pmatrix}. U(z)=​z12​z1​z2​(z1​z3​+(γ−1)z22​/2)/γ​​,F(z)=​z1​z2​((γ+1)z22​/2+(γ−1)z1​z3​)/γz2​z3​​​.

Both maps are quadratic. Their midpoint Jacobians B=∂U/∂z and C=∂F/∂z therefore satisfy ΔU=B(z̄)Δz and ΔF=C(z̄)Δz exactly. Consequently Ã=C(z̄)B(z̄)⁻¹ has the jump property. Ratios of z̄ give

u~=ρLuL+ρRuRρL+ρR,H~=ρLHL+ρRHRρL+ρR,c~2=(γ−1)(H~−u~2/2). \widetilde u=\frac{\sqrt{\rho_L}u_L+\sqrt{\rho_R}u_R}{\sqrt{\rho_L}+\sqrt{\rho_R}},\quad \widetilde H=\frac{\sqrt{\rho_L}H_L+\sqrt{\rho_R}H_R}{\sqrt{\rho_L}+\sqrt{\rho_R}},\quad \widetilde c^2=(\gamma-1)(\widetilde H-\widetilde u^2/2). u=ρL​​+ρR​​ρL​​uL​+ρR​​uR​​,H=ρL​​+ρR​​ρL​​HL​+ρR​​HR​​,c2=(γ−1)(H−u2/2).

At equal states, the chain rule gives CB⁻¹=∂F/∂U. The independently constructed eigenbasis has speeds ũ−c̃,ũ,ũ+c̃. Since c̃>0, its three eigenvectors span the state space. We check the parameter-vector matrix against this eigenbasis, the analytic Jacobian, and 2000 deterministic physical state pairs.

If ΔF=sΔU for a single nonzero Rankine–Hugoniot jump, then ÃΔU=sΔU: the jump lies in the speed-s eigenspace. The unmodified Roe flux consequently recognizes isolated contact/shock jumps. This does not make every reconstructed, time-discretized shock calculation exact. Smoothing |λ| changes the flux without changing the matrix identity, and can smear a stationary shock.

An expansion discontinuity can also satisfy the jump relation. Our reversed stationary normal-shock pair passes Property U but the raw Roe flux differs from the entropy Riemann reference. This is a numerical counterexample to confusing the jump property with entropy selection. The entropy fix is an additional design choice; neither gives a multidimensional carbuncle guarantee.

python scripts/build_shock_robustness.py saves the matrix checks, moving and stationary shocks, a contact and the expansion counterexample in the diagnostic manifest.

Rotated Riemann sources: Ren (2003), Roe–Nishikawa et al. (2005), Nishikawa–Kitamura (2008) and the atlas experiment

ale.title: Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian methods
ale.html:
Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian methods

Eulerian cells stay fixed while fluid crosses their faces. Lagrangian cells move with the fluid. In ALE, the mesh velocity w can be chosen independently of the fluid velocity u. Hirt, Amsden, and Cook (1974) provide a classical all-speed ALE formulation.

The flux is relative to the moving face#

Reynolds transport gives, for a moving control volume K(t),

ddt∫K(t)U dV+∫∂K(t)[F(U)⋅n−(w⋅n)U]dS=0. \frac{d}{dt}\int_{K(t)}U\,dV +\int_{\partial K(t)}\left[F(U)\cdot n-(w\cdot n)U\right]dS=0. dtd​∫K(t)​UdV+∫∂K(t)​[F(U)⋅n−(w⋅n)U]dS=0.

With w = 0 this is Eulerian. Choosing the normal mesh speed equal to the fluid normal speed gives the Lagrangian mass-flux limit. Pressure still transfers momentum and energy across a material face; setting mass flux to zero does not set every Euler flux to zero.

Geometry must obey a conservation law too#

For a uniform state to remain uniform, changing cell volumes and face motion must agree:

d∣K∣dt=∫∂Kw⋅n dS. \frac{d|K|}{dt}=\int_{\partial K}w\cdot n\,dS. dtd∣K∣​=∫∂K​w⋅ndS.

Its discrete counterpart is the geometric conservation law (GCL). A mesh-motion routine and a flow update that use inconsistent swept volumes can create a spurious flow from constant data, even if each looks accurate separately.

A reproducible one-step check#

numart.geometry.moving_volume_uniform_test deforms faces on [0,1] by a smooth sinusoidal displacement with fixed endpoints. Face velocity is the actual displacement divided by delta t. For constant scalar q, it updates the extensive quantity Vq with relative flux (a−w)q and divides by the new volume. The same displacement appears in both operations.

import numpy as np
from numart.geometry import moving_volume_uniform_test
old_faces, new_faces, q = moving_volume_uniform_test(phase=0.8)
print(np.max(np.abs(q - 1)))

Uniform-state preservation is checked to roundoff over several deformation phases. The amplitude restriction ensures positive cell widths. This is a 1D moving-volume identity check, not an ALE Euler solver or a test of accuracy for nonuniform data.

Mesh motion, remapping, and distortion#

A complete ALE method may move vertices, solve a Lagrangian or relative-flux step, and remap to a better mesh. Conservative remapping, mesh tangling, boundary motion, and temporal consistency require additional tests. A remap that preserves total mass can still violate positivity or fail to preserve a constant state.

Use the mesh chapter to separate topology from motion, and the coordinate chapter to distinguish moving control volumes from changing tensor bases. Neither replacing x by r nor moving plotted vertices automatically constructs an ALE method.

basis-functions.title: Orthogonal polynomials and mesh basis functions
basis-functions.html:
Orthogonal polynomials and mesh basis functions

A mesh supplies cells, geometry and connectivity. A basis supplies the functions used to represent a field on those cells. The choice of basis is separate from cell shape and variable staggering. The basis notebook makes modes, nodes and their mass matrices visible. The existing DG advection example already uses Legendre modes internally; this chapter exposes the algebra behind it.

Start on a reference element#

Map a physical interval of length h and center x_c to a reference interval:

x=xc+Jξ,J=h/2,−1≤ξ≤1,uh(x)=∑j=0pajϕj(ξ). x=x_c+J\xi,\qquad J=h/2,\qquad -1\leq\xi\leq1, \qquad u_h(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{p}a_j\phi_j(\xi). x=xc​+Jξ,J=h/2,−1≤ξ≤1,uh​(x)=j=0∑p​aj​ϕj​(ξ).

The p+1 coefficients are element degrees of freedom. In a continuous finite-element method, neighboring elements share selected boundary degrees of freedom. DG keeps independent element coefficients and couples traces through numerical fluxes. A local polynomial basis can serve either formulation.

For constant material coefficients and an affine map, the element mass and diffusion matrices are

Mij=J∫−11ϕiϕj dξ,Kij=J−1∫−11ϕi′ϕj′ dξ. M_{ij}=J\int_{-1}^{1}\phi_i\phi_j\,d\xi, \qquad K_{ij}=J^{-1}\int_{-1}^{1}\phi_i'\phi_j'\,d\xi. Mij​=J∫−11​ϕi​ϕj​dξ,Kij​=J−1∫−11​ϕi′​ϕj′​dξ.

Curved maps introduce a variable Jacobian; variable density or coefficients also change these integrals. Reference-element orthogonality alone then does not make the physical matrix diagonal.

Legendre modes and orthonormal modes#

With unit weight on [-1,1], the Legendre family satisfies

P0=1,P1=ξ,P2=(3ξ2−1)/2,(n+1)Pn+1=(2n+1)ξPn−nPn−1, P_0=1,\quad P_1=\xi,\quad P_2=(3\xi^2-1)/2, \qquad (n+1)P_{n+1}=(2n+1)\xi P_n-nP_{n-1}, P0​=1,P1​=ξ,P2​=(3ξ2−1)/2,(n+1)Pn+1​=(2n+1)ξPn​−nPn−1​,
∫−11PiPj dξ=22i+1δij,P^i=2i+12Pi. \int_{-1}^{1}P_iP_j\,d\xi=\frac{2}{2i+1}\delta_{ij}, \qquad \widehat P_i=\sqrt{\frac{2i+1}{2}}P_i. ∫−11​Pi​Pj​dξ=2i+12​δij​,Pi​=22i+1​​Pi​.

The ordinary Legendre mass is diagonal, with unequal diagonal entries. The orthonormal reference mass is the identity. Their coefficient values differ, although both span exactly the same degree-p polynomial space. The constant mode encodes the element mean; the higher Legendre modes have zero mean. See NIST DLMF §18.3 for normalization and §18.9 for recurrence relations.

Nodal Lagrange functions represent the same space#

Choose distinct nodes and define cardinal polynomials:

ℓj(ξ)=∏k≠jξ−ξkξj−ξk,ℓj(ξi)=δij,uh=∑jujℓj. \ell_j(\xi)=\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{\xi-\xi_k}{\xi_j-\xi_k}, \qquad \ell_j(\xi_i)=\delta_{ij},\qquad u_h=\sum_j u_j\ell_j. ℓj​(ξ)=k=j∏​ξj​−ξk​ξ−ξk​​,ℓj​(ξi​)=δij​,uh​=j∑​uj​ℓj​.

Here the coefficients u_j are nodal values. In a modal expansion, the coefficients are polynomial amplitudes. For the same polynomial, the change of representation is

ui=∑jVijaj,Vij=Pj(ξi),a=V−1u. u_i=\sum_j V_{ij}a_j,\qquad V_{ij}=P_j(\xi_i),\qquad a=V^{-1}u. ui​=j∑​Vij​aj​,Vij​=Pj​(ξi​),a=V−1u.

The notebook compares equispaced nodes and Gauss–Lobatto–Legendre (GLL) nodes. It reports the condition number of this Legendre Vandermonde; that number depends on normalization and is not the condition number of a complete PDE solve. Endpoint clustering can help interpolation, but does not remove Gibbs oscillations at a jump.

Quadrature and the diagonal-mass caveat#

With p+1 points, Gauss–Legendre quadrature integrates polynomials through degree 2p+1. GLL includes the endpoints and integrates through degree 2p−1. Its interior points are the zeros of P'_p, and its weights are

wi=2p(p+1)Pp(ξi)2,p≥1. w_i=\frac{2}{p(p+1)P_p(\xi_i)^2},\qquad p\geq1. wi​=p(p+1)Pp​(ξi​)22​,p≥1.

Products of degree-p basis functions can have degree 2p. Consequently, GLL collocation gives a quadrature mass diag(w), while the exactly integrated GLL nodal mass generally has off-diagonal entries. On an affine interval with unit weight, their difference is rank one. The highest Legendre squared norm is 2/p under GLL quadrature, instead of 2/(2p+1). The notebook lets you switch between both matrices. These facts, and an efficient correction, are derived in Teukolsky's mass-matrix note.

For constant-coefficient stiffness, the polynomial degree is at most 2p−2, so the same GLL rule is sufficient. Nonlinear fluxes and variable metrics can require additional quadrature or a suitable split formulation; a diagonal mass alone is not a nonlinear stability guarantee. DLMF §3.5 explains Gaussian quadrature more generally.

Projection is different from interpolation#

An unweighted L2 Legendre projection uses integral moments:

ak=2k+12∫−11f(ξ)Pk(ξ) dξ. a_k=\frac{2k+1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}f(\xi)P_k(\xi)\,d\xi. ak​=22k+1​∫−11​f(ξ)Pk​(ξ)dξ.

Nodal interpolation instead matches f at the chosen nodes. They agree for every polynomial of degree at most p, but need not agree for other functions. For exp(ξ), the notebook shows rapidly decreasing errors as p increases. For sign(ξ), the displayed overshoot and slow convergence expose the loss of smoothness; neither approximation supplies a shock limiter. The jump is integrated on two separate half-intervals, and interpolation explicitly uses sign(0)=0. L2 errors are integrated with 80-point Gauss rules on each half.

Quadrilaterals and triangles have different polynomial spaces#

On a quadrilateral, a tensor basis takes products of one-dimensional functions:

ϕij(ξ,η)=ℓi(ξ)ℓj(η),0≤i,j≤p. \phi_{ij}(\xi,\eta)=\ell_i(\xi)\ell_j(\eta),\qquad 0\leq i,j\leq p. ϕij​(ξ,η)=ℓi​(ξ)ℓj​(η),0≤i,j≤p.

This Q_p space has (p+1)^2 functions. A triangle's total-degree P_p space has (p+1)(p+2)/2. Thus Q2 has nine degrees of freedom, while triangular P2 has six. The cell topology determines which reference map and trace connectivity are needed. DefElement's Lagrange definition distinguishes these spaces and nodal variants.

On the reference triangle (0,0), (1,0), (0,1), barycentric coordinates are λ0=1−ξ−η, λ1=ξ, λ2=η. The P1 vertex functions are λ_i. P2 has vertex functions λ_i(2λ_i−1) and edge functions 4λ_iλ_j. They form a partition of unity and reproduce quadratic fields; they are not an orthogonal basis. The notebook colors each of these six shape functions on the actual triangle.

Orthogonal modal triangle bases can instead be built from suitably weighted Jacobi polynomials in collapsed coordinates, including the Dubiner (1991) construction. A rectangular Legendre tensor product restricted to a triangle does not automatically retain orthogonality. This edition implements P1/P2 nodal triangles and quadrilateral tensor evaluation; a Dubiner implementation remains additional work.

Other orthogonal families and their measures#

Orthogonality always includes a domain and a weight. Changing either changes the inner product. The notebook also tabulates Chebyshev T modes and demonstrates their nonorthogonality under unit weight. The remaining families below are mathematical reading connections. Conventions follow DLMF §18.2 and §18.3.

  • Chebyshev T_n: T_n(cos θ)=cos(nθ), on [-1,1], weight (1−ξ²)^−1/2. Useful for endpoint-clustered spectral interpolation. They are not mutually orthogonal under the unweighted finite-element mass integral.
  • Jacobi: P_n^(α,β), weight (1−ξ)^α(1+ξ)^β on [-1,1], α,β>−1. This family includes Legendre and, after normalization, Chebyshev; weighted coordinate transforms connect it to simplex bases.
  • Hermite: physicists' H_n has weight exp(−ξ²) on the real line; probabilists' He_n uses exp(−ξ²/2). These are different conventions. Orthogonal Hermite polynomials are distinct from the endpoint value/derivative Hermite interpolation used by CIP.
  • Generalized Laguerre: L_n^(α) uses ξ^α exp(−ξ) on [0,∞), α>−1. It addresses a semi-infinite domain rather than an ordinary bounded mesh cell.
  • Fourier modes: exp(ikx) are orthogonal on a periodic interval with matching integer wave numbers. They form a global periodic basis rather than a mesh-local polynomial family; the spectral advection example uses these modes.

Verification and scope#

numart.basis supplies Legendre/Chebyshev and nodal tabulation, derivatives, affine interval matrices, GLL quadrature, projection, P1/P2 triangles and tensor products. Tests check continuous Legendre orthogonality, GLL exactness limits, cardinal interpolation, polynomial reproduction, partition of unity, derivative reproduction, the GLL summation-by-parts identity, rank-one mass difference and physical Jacobian scaling. The existing DG solver remains restricted to scalar periodic P0/P1/P2 advection.

The published reference-element source is available from the Legendre method record. Saved arrays and source hashes accompany the figure. This adds reference-element building blocks, not a general curved-mesh assembly or a higher-order fluid solver.

Continue with mesh connectivity, continuous triangular FEM, DG advection, limiters and variable staggering.

Publication scope and related entries

Links lead to existing educational code and dated verification records. This reading/translation update changes no scientific code or historical measurements and does not claim reproduction of an entire paper.

  • Legendre modal basis / orthonormal scaling
  • Lagrange nodal basis / GLL collocation

Primary publications, supporting sources and review scope

Distinguish original research, later variants, author monographs, pedagogical articles and official references. Bibliographic verification differs from consulting selected passages; neither implies a full-paper audit or numerical reproduction. Access-depth notes accompany each source.

  1. Saul A. Teukolsky (2015). Short note on the mass matrix for Gauss–Lobatto grid points. Journal of Computational Physics

    Research publication: proposal or related formulation · Bibliography checked · Consulted record

    Reviewed as a source for priority-method metadata. The individual method records distinguish reference roles, relevant full-text passages, abstracts and bibliographic checks; this does not imply a new numerical validation.

  2. Moshe Dubiner (1991). Spectral methods on triangles and other domains. Journal of Scientific Computing

    Research publication: proposal or related formulation · Bibliography checked · Consulted record

    Bibliographic identity checked against the DOI registration on 2026-11-22. Relevant abstracts or selected passages are separately identified in the detailed-reading source notes; this is not a claim of a full-paper audit or numerical reproduction.

  3. F. W. J. Olver and A. B. Olde Daalhuis and D. W. Lozier and B. I. Schneider and R. F. Boisvert and C. W. Clark and B. R. Miller and B. V. Saunders and H. S. Cohl and M. A. McClain (eds.) (2010). NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions.

    Official reference documentation · Selected source passages consulted · Consulted record

    Living official reference, not the original discovery papers. Sections 3.5 and 18.2/18.3/18.9 supply quadrature and orthogonal-polynomial conventions. The year is initial release, not a claim that the current version dates from 2010.

benchmarks.title: Benchmark library
benchmarks.html:
Benchmark library

For the representation behind DG and spectral examples, see orthogonal polynomials and element bases: Legendre modes, nodal transforms, quadrature, and their mass matrices.

Each 1D Problem stores the equation, domain, final time, boundaries, initial condition, reference solution, and citation keys. get_problem(name) exposes the same definition to every method. The last array axis contains variables: Euler uses (ρ,ρu,E), shallow water uses (h,hu), and isothermal flow uses (ρ,ρu).

Smooth problems#

Linear advection uses periodic [0,1], speed a, and initial data sin(2πx). The exact translated solution compares finite differences, DG, and Fourier methods. DG uses modal Legendre P0/P1/P2, upwind boundary fluxes, and SSPRK3. Distinguish the spatial order of Pp from the third-order time integrator. DG has elements × (p+1) unknowns. Fourier integrates the linear modes exactly in time; the gallery does not establish an equal-cost or equal-degree-of-freedom ranking. Nonlinear products, dealiasing, and Gibbs treatments are future work.

entropy-wave uses Euler data ρ=1+0.2sin(2πx), u=1,p=1,γ=1.4, periodic [0,1], and t=1. Only density translates, giving an exact reference for smooth accuracy and periodic conservation. Isothermal Euler has no independent energy or entropy variable and does not support this same Euler entropy-wave problem.

Shock tubes#

Sod: [0,1], x0=0.5, left (ρ,u,p)=(1,0,1), right (0.125,0,0.1), γ=1.4, and t=0.2. Boundaries use zero-gradient extrapolation; the main waves do not reach them before the final time. The exact Riemann solver finds the matching pressure by bisection and samples shocks, contacts, and rarefaction fans. Exact solutions containing a vacuum are unsupported. Sod (1978), exact-solution implementation reference.

Lax: [-5,5], x0=0, left (0.445,0.698,3.528), right (0.5,0,0.571), γ=1.4, t=1.3, and extrapolation boundaries. The Lax test and the Lax–Friedrichs algorithm are different namesakes. These are standard parameters from later literature; the original 1954 paper's table has not been directly matched here.

Shu–Osher: [-5,5], x0=-4, t=1.8, γ=1.4, left (3.857143,2.629369,10.33333), and right (1+0.2sin(5x),0,1). Ghost states are fixed to the initial conditions evaluated at the domain ends. There is no exact final-time reference; the first-edition figure compares MUSCL and WENO numerical results. Shu–Osher (1989), adopted parameters in Quokka, §3.1.5.

Low densities and Einfeldt-type tests#

double-rarefaction uses [0,1], x0=0.5, left (1,-2,0.4), right (1,2,0.4), γ=1.4, and t=0.15. This strong expansion is commonly called the 1–2–3 problem. The selected positivity test uses piecewise-constant reconstruction with HLLE. It does not transfer a positivity guarantee to high-order MUSCL or WENO. Einfeldt et al. (1991).

Shallow-water and isothermal flow#

dam-break solves flat-bottom shallow water with g=1, left h=2, right h=1, u=0, [0,1], and t=0.1. Dry beds, topographic sources, well-balanced discretization, and wetting/drying are unsupported. isothermal uses p=cs²ρ, cs=1, left ρ=1, right ρ=0.125, and u=0 on the same domain and time interval. Both use extrapolation boundaries. First-edition checks compare solvers, admissible states, and conservative form. The reference library now supplies semi-analytic Riemann states and conserved cell means for the equation gallery. The original Problem.reference callbacks for these two cases remain unset; use get_reference for the new evaluations. LeVeque (2002).

Riemann fluxes and reconstruction#

Rusanov and HLL support Euler, shallow water, and isothermal flow. HLLC, Roe, and HLLE currently support ideal-gas Euler only. HLL uses minimum/maximum local acoustic speeds; HLLE uses Einfeldt-type estimates including Roe averages. Roe applies quadratic entropy smoothing to acoustic eigenvalues with δ=0.1ã, leaving the contact eigenvalue unchanged. This is neither a low-density positivity fix nor a general entropy-stable flux construction.

MUSCL uses selectable minmod (default), Superbee, MC, van Leer, or clipped van Albada reconstruction in primitive variables; see limiters. WENO5-JS is a componentwise finite-difference implementation with pointwise fluxes and global LF splitting. A separate reconstruction chapter below adds characteristics and WENO-Z; this original solver remains unchanged. Fully discrete positivity preservation is still future work. A separate advanced limiter exhibit implements TVB modified minmod and positive Euler reconstruction scaling; neither is coupled to these Euler time updates. Errors are labeled pointwise: finite-volume cell averages and finite-difference point values are not strictly interchangeable.

See MHD for Orszag–Tang definitions and limits, and elliptic problems for diffusion and Poisson cases.

Matching the benchmark to the scheme#

The original KEEP exhibit uses a smooth isentropic vortex and conservation diagnostics. Its bare central flux has no shock stabilization and is not presented as a Sod/DMR solver. The movie guide separates those smooth computations from shock-capturing and MHD movies, and keeps steady fields as still images.

Equation-first scalar comparisons#

The equation gallery adds Burgers and LWR traffic Riemann problems with exact cell-integrated references, plus advection and heat mode tests. It also connects the existing Sod, wet dam-break and isothermal baselines, with each reference convention explicitly labeled.

Expanded reconstruction and flux tests#

The new reconstruction chapter and interactive comparison add limited parabolic FV, conservative characteristics, FD WENO-Z and an explicit AUSM-family baseline. The original code described above remains a componentwise baseline. Planar shock sensitivity and Roe's Property U have separate verification.

biological-models.title: Biological model equations and numerical verification
biological-models.html:
Biological model equations and numerical verification

Run and validate small model examples

The 22-family survey links scoped examples of logistic growth, closed SIR, linear reaction–diffusion, linear Schnakenberg onset, finite-amplitude nonlinear evolution and post-growth 1D patterns, plus spatially uniform FitzHugh–Nagumo. This does not implement all 22 families or Hodgkin–Huxley.

  • Reaction-diffusion: separate second-order space and fourth-order time
  • Turing instability: linear growth and small-amplitude patterns
  • FitzHugh-Nagumo: pulse excitation, recovery and an independent ODE reference
  • Finite-amplitude Schnakenberg transient: nonlinearity and independent reference
  • Near-saturated Schnakenberg pattern: near-stationarity and grid/time convergence
  • Lie–Trotter versus Strang on the same nonlinear reaction–diffusion input

Analytic references for logistic/linear reaction–diffusion, independent DOP853 for SIR/FHN and matrix exponentials for linear Turing growth. New nonlinear Schnakenberg checks distinguish an independent dealiased Fourier–Galerkin/Radau reference from Radau on the same finite-difference semidiscretization used to isolate time error.

Read about nonlinear evolution, post-growth patterns and independent references · Implementation scope, results and gaps

This survey selects 22 biological and biologically motivated model families, from population growth to stochastic gene regulation and fluid–structure coupling. It expands the equation map beyond conservation-law CFD. The 22-family survey links scoped examples of logistic growth, closed SIR, linear reaction–diffusion, linear Schnakenberg onset, finite-amplitude nonlinear evolution and post-growth 1D patterns, plus spatially uniform FitzHugh–Nagumo. This does not implement all 22 families or Hodgkin–Huxley.

The equations below use conventional simplified or normalized forms. A source identifies the model lineage, not a claim that every coefficient and variable matches that paper. The structured catalog retains references, numerical issues, verification targets and scope for each entry. The selection emphasizes numerical variety, rather than a comprehensive review of present-day mathematical biology. Sources checked on 6 November 2026.

Which biological questions exercise which algorithms#

  • Population growth and ecology: logistic, predator–prey, Fisher fronts, cross-diffusion and replicator dynamics test positive states, invariant sets, long-time behavior and spatial invasion.
  • Demography and epidemics: age transport and compartment models test renewal boundaries, balances, nonnegative compartments and thresholds.
  • Biochemistry and metabolism: enzyme kinetics and Monod growth connect stiff ODEs, conservation laws and reduced models.
  • Morphogenesis: Turing analysis, Gierer–Meinhardt, Schnakenberg and Gray–Scott separate physical instability from numerical pattern selection.
  • Excitation: Hodgkin–Huxley, FitzHugh–Nagumo and Aliev–Panfilov connect stiff reactions to pulse conduction, refractoriness and spiral waves.
  • Gene regulation and noise: delayed feedback, toggles, repressilators and the chemical master equation need history interpolation, bifurcation analysis or jump-process simulation.
  • Biomechanics: a fluid–elastic structure requires constitutive forces and a coupling discretization in addition to fluid equations.

Existing diffusion and elliptic methods, FEM, sparse/Newton methods, stiff integrators and incompressible projection supply useful numerical building blocks. Their current tests do not verify these new biological systems.

Historical model catalog#

Dates identify an early source or a selected development, not an exclusive priority claim. Later spatial extensions, reductions and translations are identified with their individual entries.

01 · 1838 · Logistic population growth#

Logistic fixed-input / analytic checks available. Density-limited growth with carrying capacity K. It is the simplest biological ODE baseline.

N˙=rN(1−N/K). \dot N=rN(1-N/K). N˙=rN(1−N/K).

Numerical issue. Positivity, preservation of equilibria and overshoot of K; an accurate-looking curve can still violate the invariant interval.

Proposed verification. Compare with N(t)=K/[1+(K/N0−1)exp(−rt)] for N0>0; measure temporal order and behavior near 0 and K.

Model convention. The linked original is the later 1847 memoir; the 1838 note itself was not audited. The differential equation is not the discrete logistic map.

Sources: Verhulst, Pierre-François (1847).

02 · 1913 · Michaelis–Menten and full enzyme kinetics#

Biochemical reactions · Survey only. Enzyme saturation; the full mass-action system resolves the transient complex C, while the rate law eliminates a fast variable.

E+S⇌k−1k1C⟶k2E+P,v=Vmax⁡S/(KM+S). E+S\mathrel{\mathop{\rightleftharpoons}^{k_1}_{k_{-1}}}C\mathrel{\mathop{\longrightarrow}^{k_2}}E+P,\qquad v=V_{\max}S/(K_M+S). E+S⇌k−1​k1​​C⟶k2​E+P,v=Vmax​S/(KM​+S).

Numerical issue. Fast initial layers and stiffness; full and reduced models have different validity regimes. Under the usual quasi-steady approximation KM=(k−1+k2)/k1.

Proposed verification. Check E+C and S+C+P conservation in the closed mechanism. Compare reduced and full systems as enzyme/substrate scales vary, rather than calling the reduction exact.

Model convention. The 1913 rapid-equilibrium interpretation and the 1925 quasi-steady-state derivation must remain distinct.

Sources: Michaelis–Menten (1913; via the 2011 translation), Briggs, George E. and Haldane, J. B. S. (1925), Johnson, Kenneth A. and Goody, Roger S. (2011).

03 · 1920 · Lotka–Volterra predator–prey#

Population and ecology · Survey only. Coupled prey growth and predation; a phase-plane and long-time integration test.

x˙=αx−βxy,y˙=δxy−γy. \dot x=\alpha x-\beta xy,\qquad\dot y=\delta xy-\gamma y. x˙=αx−βxy,y˙​=δxy−γy.

Numerical issue. Positive states and artificial damping or growth of closed orbits. Periodic orbits of this idealized system are not attracting limit cycles.

Proposed verification. Monitor H=δx−γ ln(x)+βy−α ln(y) for positive x,y, and compare orbit drift under step refinement.

Sources: Lotka, Alfred J. (1920), Volterra, Vito (1926).

04 · 1926 · McKendrick age-structured population#

Structured population transport · Survey only. Individuals move through age a at unit speed; newborns enter through a nonlocal renewal boundary.

∂tn+∂an=−μ(a)n,n(0,t)=∫0∞b(a)n(a,t) da. \partial_t n+\partial_a n=-\mu(a)n,\qquad n(0,t)=\int_0^\infty b(a)n(a,t)\,da. ∂t​n+∂a​n=−μ(a)n,n(0,t)=∫0∞​b(a)n(a,t)da.

Numerical issue. Upwind/FV transport in age, birth-boundary quadrature and truncation of the infinite age interval.

Proposed verification. Use characteristic survival along cohorts and check d∫n da/dt=births−deaths, including any artificial oldest-age outflow.

Model convention. This is the classical age-transport form; the later von Foerster lineage is acknowledged without treating its date as the first appearance.

Sources: McKendrick, A. G. (1926).

05 · 1927 · SIR and SEIR compartment models#

Closed-SIR example available; SEIR unimplemented. Closed, well-mixed normalized population fractions. SEIR adds an exposed compartment and a progression rate.

s˙=−βsi,i˙=βsi−γi,r˙=γi,s+i+r=1. \dot s=-\beta si,\quad\dot i=\beta si-\gamma i,\quad\dot r=\gamma i,\quad s+i+r=1. s˙=−βsi,i˙=βsi−γi,r˙=γi,s+i+r=1.

Numerical issue. Nonnegative compartments, invariant total population and correct resolution of epidemic peak times.

Proposed verification. Check total 1 and i+s−(γ/β)ln(s) for β>0,s>0; compare early growth rate βs0−γ and final-size relation in the closed SIR specialization.

Model convention. The original general epidemic framework is broader than this SIR specialization. Population-count and fraction conventions give different β definitions.

Sources: Kermack, W. O. and McKendrick, A. G. (1927).

06 · 1937 · Fisher–KPP invasion front#

Population and ecology · Survey only. Spatial spread of an invading population or advantageous allele, represented by a reaction–diffusion front.

ut=DΔu+ru(1−u),0≤u≤1. u_t=D\Delta u+ru(1-u),\qquad 0\leq u\leq1. ut​=DΔu+ru(1−u),0≤u≤1.

Numerical issue. Spatial and temporal front-speed errors; leading-edge resolution, positivity and finite-domain boundary contamination.

Proposed verification. Use the Ablowitz–Zeppetella exact front at c=5√(Dr/6), or test the minimal speed 2√(Dr) only with the appropriate steep initial-data regime on a sufficiently large domain.

Model convention. Fisher–KPP is a conventional family name; the independent KPP 1937 original remains an archival follow-up. The exact special speed is not the minimal speed.

Sources: Fisher, R. A. (1937), Ablowitz, Mark J. and Zeppetella, Anthony (1979).

07 · 1949 · Monod growth and chemostat#

Biochemical reactions · Survey only. Nutrient-limited biomass X, substrate S, yield Y and chemostat dilution d; d=0 gives a closed batch model.

μ(S)=μmax⁡SKS+S,X˙=(μ(S)−d)X,S˙=d(Sin−S)−μ(S)X/Y. \mu(S)=\mu_{\max}\frac{S}{K_S+S},\quad\dot X=(\mu(S)-d)X,\quad\dot S=d(S_{in}-S)-\mu(S)X/Y. μ(S)=μmax​KS​+SS​,X˙=(μ(S)−d)X,S˙=d(Sin​−S)−μ(S)X/Y.

Numerical issue. Washout near a threshold, disparate resource/growth scales, positivity and the distinction between yield and rate constants.

Proposed verification. For d=0 check S+X/Y. For d>0 use d(S+X/Y)/dt=d[Sin−(S+X/Y)] and verify the washout equilibrium.

Model convention. This writes one constant-yield extension of saturation growth, not a universal metabolic model.

Sources: Monod, Jacques (1949).

08 · 1952 · Hodgkin–Huxley membrane dynamics#

Excitable systems · Survey only. Voltage and gating variables z=m,h,n describe an ionic excitable membrane. A cable extension adds spatial axial current.

CmV˙=Iapp−gˉNam3h(V−ENa)−gˉKn4(V−EK)−gL(V−EL),z˙=αz(V)(1−z)−βz(V)z. C_m\dot V=I_{app}-\bar g_{Na}m^3h(V-E_{Na})-\bar g_Kn^4(V-E_K)-g_L(V-E_L),\quad\dot z=\alpha_z(V)(1-z)-\beta_z(V)z. Cm​V˙=Iapp​−gˉ​Na​m3h(V−ENa​)−gˉ​K​n4(V−EK​)−gL​(V−EL​),z˙=αz​(V)(1−z)−βz​(V)z.

Numerical issue. Stiff gates, removable singularities in rate formulas, gating bounds, voltage/current sign and temperature conventions.

Proposed verification. Select an explicitly versioned CellML/reference convention, verify resting equilibrium and gate relaxation at clamped voltage, then refine spike time and waveform.

Model convention. The original squid-axon model is not a calibrated human cardiac model. No single rate parameter set is selected by this survey.

Sources: Hodgkin, A. L. and Huxley, A. F. (1952).

09 · 1952 · Turing reaction–diffusion framework#

Separate scoped checks of linear onset, nonlinear evolution and post-growth patterns for fixed 1D Schnakenberg systems. A framework for diffusion-driven pattern onset around a homogeneous reaction equilibrium, not a unique choice of f and g.

ut=DuΔu+f(u,v),vt=DvΔv+g(u,v). u_t=D_u\Delta u+f(u,v),\qquad v_t=D_v\Delta v+g(u,v). ut​=Du​Δu+f(u,v),vt​=Dv​Δv+g(u,v).

Numerical issue. Physical versus numerical instability, domain eigenmodes and errors in the discrete Laplacian dispersion relation.

Proposed verification. For a selected kinetic law compare eigenvalues of J−k²diag(Du,Dv) with early-time Fourier-mode growth. Show that the k=0 reaction equilibrium is stable before asserting diffusion-driven instability.

Model convention. A spot image or unequal diffusion coefficients alone do not establish a Turing mechanism. Boundary conditions determine the available modes.

Sources: Turing, Alan M. (1952).

10 · 1961 · FitzHugh–Nagumo excitation and recovery#

FHN excitation/recovery ODE and time refinement available; full HH unimplemented. A normalized fast excitation/slow recovery model for pulses, refractoriness and spiral waves when extended in space.

vt=DΔv+v−v3/3−w+I,wt=ϵ(v+a−bw). v_t=D\Delta v+v-v^3/3-w+I,\qquad w_t=\epsilon(v+a-bw). vt​=DΔv+v−v3/3−w+I,wt​=ϵ(v+a−bw).

Numerical issue. Stiff time-scale separation, splitting error, wave-speed convergence and numerical wave breakup.

Proposed verification. Check ODE fixed points/nullclines and small-perturbation eigenvalues first; then refine a 1D pulse before a 2D spiral movie.

Model convention. This is a common normalized variant; cubic coefficients, recovery signs and nondimensionalization differ between formulations.

Sources: FitzHugh, Richard (1961), Nagumo, Jinichi and Arimoto, Suguru and Yoshizawa, Shuji (1962).

11 · 1970 · Keller–Segel chemotaxis#

Chemotaxis · Survey only. Cell density n drifts up a chemoattractant gradient; τc=0 gives an elliptic chemical subproblem.

nt=DnΔn−χ∇⋅(n∇c),τcct=DcΔc+αn−λc. n_t=D_n\Delta n-\chi\nabla\cdot(n\nabla c),\qquad\tau_c c_t=D_c\Delta c+\alpha n-\lambda c. nt​=Dn​Δn−χ∇⋅(n∇c),τc​ct​=Dc​Δc+αn−λc.

Numerical issue. Cross-coupled flux, positivity, mass conservation and concentrated peaks; spurious undershoots must not be mistaken for physical aggregation or blowup.

Proposed verification. With zero total cell flux check ∫n conservation, homogeneous equilibria and linear growth; refine the peak and domain before discussing singularity. Use manufactured smooth solutions before aggregation cases.

Model convention. This is a common two-field reduction of a more detailed original formulation. Blowup thresholds depend on dimension, domain, boundary and chemical dynamics.

Sources: Keller, Evelyn F. and Segel, Lee A. (1970).

12 · 1972 · Gierer–Meinhardt activator–inhibitor#

Pattern formation · Survey only. A representative simplified short-range activation/long-range inhibition model.

at=DaΔa+ρa2/h−μa+σa,ht=DhΔh+ρha2−νh. a_t=D_a\Delta a+\rho a^2/h-\mu a+\sigma_a,\qquad h_t=D_h\Delta h+\rho_h a^2-\nu h. at​=Da​Δa+ρa2/h−μa+σa​,ht​=Dh​Δh+ρh​a2−νh.

Numerical issue. The inhibitor denominator can become singular; positive h, narrow peaks and reaction stiffness require explicit treatment.

Proposed verification. Choose a positive homogeneous equilibrium, check its dispersion relation and inhibitor positivity, then refine spike width and pattern wavelength.

Model convention. Source densities, saturation and baseline production vary across the model family. This simplified formula is not a verbatim transcription of every original variant.

Sources: Gierer, Alfred and Meinhardt, Hans (1972).

13 · 1972 · Fluid–elastic structure and immersed boundaries#

Biomechanics · Survey only. Fluid coupled to a deformable structure; biological examples include valves and membranes, once a force/constitutive law is supplied.

ρ(ut+u⋅∇u)=−∇p+μΔu+f,∇⋅u=0,Xt=u(X,t). \rho(\boldsymbol u_t+\boldsymbol u\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol u)=-\nabla p+\mu\Delta\boldsymbol u+\boldsymbol f,\quad\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol u=0,\quad\boldsymbol X_t=\boldsymbol u(\boldsymbol X,t). ρ(ut​+u⋅∇u)=−∇p+μΔu+f,∇⋅u=0,Xt​=u(X,t).

Numerical issue. Stiff elastic forces, pressure projection, Eulerian–Lagrangian interpolation/spreading and volume leakage.

Proposed verification. Specify elastic energy and force before solving. Check force transfer, adjoint interpolation/spreading, fluid divergence and enclosed-volume drift on a simple relaxing boundary.

Model convention. Immersed boundary is a numerical coupling method, not itself a closed biological constitutive equation. The existing periodic MAC solver does not implement this coupling.

Sources: Peskin, Charles S. (1972).

14 · 1977 · Chemical master equation and Gillespie SSA#

Stochastic reaction networks · Survey only. Integer molecule counts, reaction jumps νj and propensities aj; SSA samples paths of this continuous-time Markov model.

∂tP(n,t)=∑j[aj(n−νj)P(n−νj,t)−aj(n)P(n,t)]. \partial_t P(\boldsymbol n,t)=\sum_j\left[a_j(\boldsymbol n-\boldsymbol\nu_j)P(\boldsymbol n-\boldsymbol\nu_j,t)-a_j(\boldsymbol n)P(\boldsymbol n,t)\right]. ∂t​P(n,t)=j∑​[aj​(n−νj​)P(n−νj​,t)−aj​(n)P(n,t)].

Numerical issue. Correct combinatorial propensities, event ordering, absorbing states and statistical error; tau-leaping is a separate approximation.

Proposed verification. Use immigration–death reactions ∅→X at constant rate k and X→∅ at rate γn: stationary counts are Poisson(k/γ). Compare ensemble mean, variance and distribution with confidence intervals.

Model convention. The 1977 paper is a foundational SSA reference, not a priority claim for all master equations. SSA is a solver; the reaction network is the model. A seed documents a trajectory, not an ensemble validation.

Sources: Gillespie, Daniel T. (1977).

15 · 1977 · Mackey–Glass delayed physiological feedback#

Delay and gene regulation · Survey only. Delayed feedback in a normalized physiological control model; delay can change stability and oscillatory behavior.

x˙(t)=βx(t−τ)1+x(t−τ)p−γx(t). \dot x(t)=\frac{\beta x(t-\tau)}{1+x(t-\tau)^p}-\gamma x(t). x˙(t)=1+x(t−τ)pβx(t−τ)​−γx(t).

Numerical issue. A history function over [−τ,0], delayed interpolation, propagated derivative discontinuities and delay-aware adaptive stepping.

Proposed verification. Check the τ=0 ODE limit, a constant equilibrium history and a manufactured forced solution. Compare long-time statistics rather than expecting chaotic trajectories to match pointwise indefinitely.

Model convention. A scalar initial value alone is insufficient. The delayed ODE is distinct from a spatial reaction–diffusion model.

Sources: Mackey, Michael C. and Glass, Leon (1977).

16 · 1978 · Replicator evolutionary game dynamics#

Evolutionary dynamics · Survey only. Strategy fractions reproduce according to relative payoff in a specified matrix game.

x˙i=xi[(Ax)i−xTAx],xi≥0,∑ixi=1. \dot x_i=x_i[(A\boldsymbol x)_i-\boldsymbol x^TA\boldsymbol x],\qquad x_i\geq0,\quad\sum_i x_i=1. x˙i​=xi​[(Ax)i​−xTAx],xi​≥0,i∑​xi​=1.

Numerical issue. Preserving the probability simplex, behavior near extinction boundaries, neutral cycles versus attracting equilibria.

Proposed verification. Check simplex conservation, exact invariant faces and an analytically chosen game equilibrium; use the appropriate game-specific invariant or Lyapunov function.

Model convention. No universal Lyapunov function or equivalence of fixed point and evolutionarily stable strategy is assumed.

Sources: Taylor, Peter D. and Jonker, Leo B. (1978).

17 · 1979 · Schnakenberg reaction–diffusion#

Finite-amplitude nonlinear evolution and post-growth patterns compared with independent references and separate space/time refinement; no general pattern-selection claim. A simple autocatalytic kinetic law extended in space, useful for reproducible Turing-onset tests.

ut=DuΔu+a−u+u2v,vt=DvΔv+b−u2v. u_t=D_u\Delta u+a-u+u^2v,\qquad v_t=D_v\Delta v+b-u^2v. ut​=Du​Δu+a−u+u2v,vt​=Dv​Δv+b−u2v.

Numerical issue. Reaction stiffness, positive concentrations and the distinction between kinetic Hopf and spatial Turing instabilities.

Proposed verification. Check u*=a+b, v*=b/(a+b)², then compare mode-growth rates with the linearized discrete and continuum operators under fixed boundaries.

Model convention. A mathematical chemical pattern model; matching a visual biological pattern does not calibrate it to a tissue.

Sources: Schnakenberg, Jürgen (1979).

18 · 1979 · Shigesada–Kawasaki–Teramoto cross-diffusion#

Population and ecology · Survey only. Competition with density-dependent self- and cross-dispersal can produce spatial segregation.

ut=Δ[(d1+α11u+α12v)u]+u(a1−b1u−c1v),vt=Δ[(d2+α21u+α22v)v]+v(a2−b2u−c2v). u_t=\Delta[(d_1+\alpha_{11}u+\alpha_{12}v)u]+u(a_1-b_1u-c_1v),\quad v_t=\Delta[(d_2+\alpha_{21}u+\alpha_{22}v)v]+v(a_2-b_2u-c_2v). ut​=Δ[(d1​+α11​u+α12​v)u]+u(a1​−b1​u−c1​v),vt​=Δ[(d2​+α21​u+α22​v)v]+v(a2​−b2​u−c2​v).

Numerical issue. A coupled nonlinear diffusion matrix, loss of simple scalar maximum-principle arguments, positivity and entropy-compatible discretization.

Proposed verification. Start with manufactured smooth solutions and constant-state equilibria. With reactions removed and no normal flux, conserve each species mass; check coefficient assumptions before claiming an entropy law.

Model convention. The displayed homogeneous-environment reduction omits the original environmental-potential terms. It is not equivalent to two independent scalar diffusion equations.

Sources: Shigesada, Nanako and Kawasaki, Kohkichi and Teramoto, Ei (1979).

19 · 1983 · Gray–Scott spatial autocatalysis#

Pattern formation · Survey only. A chemical feed/decay model whose spatial extension supports diverse spot and wave patterns.

ut=DuΔu−uv2+F(1−u),vt=DvΔv+uv2−(F+k)v. u_t=D_u\Delta u-uv^2+F(1-u),\qquad v_t=D_v\Delta v+uv^2-(F+k)v. ut​=Du​Δu−uv2+F(1−u),vt​=Dv​Δv+uv2−(F+k)v.

Numerical issue. Sensitivity to F,k, diffusion, domain and finite-amplitude initial perturbations; grid-scale patterns and floating-point variation can affect long-time morphology.

Proposed verification. Record every parameter and the perturbation seed. Verify the homogeneous (1,0) state and early perturbation response, then perform grid/time refinement of quantitative observables.

Model convention. 1983 is the well-mixed CSTR source; Pearson 1993 is the spatial pattern reference. Spot division does not by itself demonstrate cell division or a linear Turing instability.

Sources: Gray, Peter and Scott, Stephen K. (1983), Pearson, John E. (1993).

20 · 1996 · Aliev–Panfilov cardiac excitation#

Excitable systems · Survey only. A reduced phenomenological excitation/recovery model for cardiac waves and restitution.

ut=DΔu−ku(u−a)(u−1)−uv,vt=(ϵ0+μ1vu+μ2)[−v−ku(u−b−1)]. u_t=D\Delta u-ku(u-a)(u-1)-uv,\quad v_t=\left(\epsilon_0+\frac{\mu_1v}{u+\mu_2}\right)[-v-ku(u-b-1)]. ut​=DΔu−ku(u−a)(u−1)−uv,vt​=(ϵ0​+u+μ2​μ1​v​)[−v−ku(u−b−1)].

Numerical issue. Stiff recovery, denominator behavior and sensitivity of wave speed/restitution to resolution and time splitting.

Proposed verification. Select a specific model encoding and parameters; establish single-cell and 1D conduction convergence before 2D reentry. Compare a restitution curve, not only a spiral image.

Model convention. Monodomain/bidomain tissue models add conductivity tensors and, for bidomain, an extracellular elliptic constraint. They are not automatically included by this two-variable model.

Sources: Aliev, R. R. and Panfilov, A. V. (1996).

21 · 2000 · Repressilator mRNA–protein network#

Delay and gene regulation · Survey only. Three repressing genes form a cyclic network; retaining mRNA and protein gives six state variables.

m˙i=α1+pi−1n+α0−mi,p˙i=β(mi−pi),i=1,2,3 cyclic. \dot m_i=\frac{\alpha}{1+p_{i-1}^n}+\alpha_0-m_i,\quad\dot p_i=\beta(m_i-p_i),\qquad i=1,2,3\ \text{cyclic}. m˙i​=1+pi−1n​α​+α0​−mi​,p˙​i​=β(mi​−pi​),i=1,2,3 cyclic.

Numerical issue. Multiple degradation scales, oscillation onset, phase error and differences between deterministic cycles and noisy individual-cell behavior.

Proposed verification. Check the symmetric equilibrium and its linear stability. Compare period and amplitude under time refinement after a stated transient.

Model convention. The six-variable form is distinct from a reduced three-protein oscillator; oscillations are parameter-dependent.

Sources: Elowitz, Michael B. and Leibler, Stanislas (2000).

22 · 2000 · Genetic toggle switch#

Delay and gene regulation · Survey only. Mutual repression produces a possible bistable genetic switch in a normalized model.

u˙=α11+vp−u,v˙=α21+uq−v. \dot u=\frac{\alpha_1}{1+v^p}-u,\qquad\dot v=\frac{\alpha_2}{1+u^q}-v. u˙=1+vpα1​​−u,v˙=1+uqα2​​−v.

Numerical issue. Parameter-dependent bistability, saddle separatrices, continuation and sensitivity to perturbations near basin boundaries.

Proposed verification. Find all positive equilibria and their Jacobian eigenvalues; verify hysteresis with sufficiently slow continuation and multiple initial conditions.

Model convention. Bistability is not guaranteed for arbitrary Hill exponents or production rates. Induction, mRNA dynamics and noise are additional model choices.

Sources: Gardner, Timothy S. and Cantor, Charles R. and Collins, James J. (2000).

A verification path before attractive movies#

A practical first sequence is logistic/SIR → full enzyme kinetics → Fisher front → FitzHugh–Nagumo pulse → Schnakenberg modes → Keller–Segel aggregation. Predator–prey can run alongside the Hamiltonian notebook as a long-time invariant test, while a birth–death SSA provides the first stochastic branch. Gray–Scott is a later visually useful chemical exhibit, with explicit feed rates, spatial scales, initial perturbation and source attribution. This order is an implementation proposal, separate from the historical order.

An exact nonlinear front#

For the scaled Fisher equation, the special front of Ablowitz–Zeppetella (1979) gives a particularly useful deterministic reference:

u(x,t)=[1+exp⁡(r6D(x−ct−x0))]−2,c=5Dr6. u(x,t)=\left[1+\exp\left(\sqrt{\frac r{6D}}(x-ct-x_0)\right)\right]^{-2}, \qquad c=5\sqrt{\frac{Dr}{6}}. u(x,t)=[1+exp(6Dr​​(x−ct−x0​))]−2,c=56Dr​​.

A finite interval should use matching time-dependent analytic boundary data, or put boundaries far enough away and quantify the truncation effect. Compare front location, profile norms and temporal/spatial refinement separately. The special explicit front travels faster than the minimal-speed front; confusing these two reference problems would produce a false solver error.

Pattern onset is a quantitative test#

For a chosen two-species reaction equilibrium, form its Jacobian J. On the continuum, a Fourier mode with wavevector k evolves under

L(k)=J−∣k∣2diag⁡(Du,Dv). L(k)=J-|k|^2\operatorname{diag}(D_u,D_v). L(k)=J−∣k∣2diag(Du​,Dv​).

On a uniform square grid with a centered Laplacian, replace |k|² by

κh2=4h2[sin⁡2(kxh/2)+sin⁡2(kyh/2)]. \kappa_h^2=\frac4{h^2} \left[\sin^2(k_xh/2)+\sin^2(k_yh/2)\right]. κh2​=h24​[sin2(kx​h/2)+sin2(ky​h/2)].

Seed one small eigenmode, measure its early exponential growth and compare both dispersion relations. A stable k=0 reaction system and an unstable nonzero mode diagnose the selected diffusion-driven instability; nonlinear late-time spots alone do not. Schnakenberg supplies a simple kinetic law for this exercise; it should not be silently substituted for Turing's own example. Periodic and zero-flux boundaries admit different mode sets.

Preserve the model before judging the method#

Each future run should specify dimensional or normalized variables, the full parameter set, boundary/initial conditions, units, random seed where relevant, model version and source. Balances include boundary flux and source terms: not every biological reaction–diffusion problem conserves each species mass. Positivity fixes that clip values may change totals and extinction thresholds. An implicit diffusion step alone does not prove positivity of a split update.

For stochastic networks, distinguish discretization/model approximation from finite-ensemble sampling uncertainty. For nonlinear reaction networks the ODE solution need not equal the exact stochastic mean. For delayed equations, record the history function and interpolation rule. For biochemical reductions, measure the model-reduction error separately from integration error.

Sources and further branches#

Murray's third-edition introduction (2002) provides a broad reading route across these branches. Physiome's Hodgkin–Huxley workspace and Aliev–Panfilov encoding are model-version references to inspect before choosing implementation parameters, rather than independent validation data.

Separate follow-up surveys could cover neural population fields, spatial stochastic reaction–diffusion, intracellular polarity and mass-conserving reaction networks, cell-cycle size structure, vertex/phase-field cell mechanics, tumor/nutrient free boundaries, and population genetics with drift. These are additional branches, not a claim that the current 22 entries exhaust biological modeling. Numerical verification against a stated equation is also different from validation against organism- or experiment-specific data.

Return to the equation gallery, the historical atlas, or the full reference catalog.

carbuncle.title: The carbuncle phenomenon
carbuncle.html:
The carbuncle phenomenon

A strong shock can develop a spurious bulge, streaks, or alternating transverse states when captured by a multidimensional numerical scheme. This carbuncle instability is a property of the discretized flow problem; a sharp-looking shock alone does not establish accuracy. Grid-aligned shocks are a particularly revealing setting.

Quirk (1994) documents failures of Godunov-type solvers and motivates switching between complementary fluxes. Pandolfi and D’Ambrosio (2001) analyze shock-related instabilities and localized remedies. Their analyses motivate the diagnostic questions below; this chapter does not claim a universal mechanism or a new stability proof.

Why a one-dimensional flux can fail in two dimensions#

A face-normal Roe flux has the form

F^n=12(Fn(UL)+Fn(UR))−12∑k∣λ~k∣ αkr~k. \widehat F_n=\tfrac12(F_n(U_L)+F_n(U_R)) -\tfrac12\sum_k |\widetilde\lambda_k|\,\alpha_k\widetilde r_k. Fn​=21​(Fn​(UL​)+Fn​(UR​))−21​k∑​∣λk​∣αk​rk​.

Its characteristic decomposition gives different dissipation to acoustic, contact, and shear waves. Near a stationary, grid-aligned shock, disturbances in neighboring rows can interact with weakly damped transverse modes and the discrete shock structure. Resolving contacts accurately and stabilizing every strong multidimensional shock are separate design demands. The entire scheme matters: reconstruction, flux, time integration, mesh, and boundaries.

Odd–even decoupling describes alternating neighboring-row behavior and is a useful shock-instability diagnostic. It is related to carbuncle studies, but the terms do not identify one identical test in every paper. The familiar blunt-body shock bulge and a perturbed planar-shock experiment have different geometries and boundary conditions.

Three different questions#

  • Entropy correction: a transonic rarefaction can be represented by an inadmissible expansion shock. Smoothing a small acoustic eigenvalue addresses this sonic-wave issue. It does not by itself certify multidimensional strong-shock stability.
  • Positivity: density and pressure must remain admissible. Wave-speed bounds, a suitable CFL restriction, and positivity-preserving reconstruction address this question. Positive states can still contain a carbuncle.
  • Transverse shock robustness: perturbations along the shock must not grow into a grid-dependent artifact. This requires its own multidimensional evidence.

The library’s 1D Roe entropy smoothing belongs to the first category. Passing Sod or the double-rarefaction test does not answer the third.

Remedies and their tradeoffs#

A two-wave HLL/HLLE flux or Rusanov flux usually adds more dissipation to contact and shear information than a contact-resolving solver. A shock sensor can blend a sharper flux with a more dissipative one locally. Rotated or multidimensional flux constructions seek dissipation in directions that a strictly face-normal treatment can miss. See Nishikawa and Kitamura (2008) for a rotated-hybrid approach.

These are design directions, not interchangeable guarantees. A sensor may also damp a physical shear layer; excessive dissipation can conceal an instability while losing the feature of interest. State the actual wave-speed estimate: this atlas’s 2D baseline uses HLL with Davis-type bounds, not an implementation of every Einfeldt HLLE variant.

What an honest comparison must measure#

Use a perturbed planar strong shock, then a blunt-body flow on a controlled grid sequence. Fix the shock Mach number, shock location relative to cell faces, perturbation amplitude and wavelength, boundary conditions, reconstruction, CFL, and final time. Compare Roe, HLL/HLLE, and a proposed hybrid under matched settings. Repeat with shifted or rotated meshes.

For periodic transverse rows, one possible alternating-density diagnostic at a selected shock-normal station is

Aπ(i,t)=∣1Ny∑j=0Ny−1(−1)j(ρi,j(t)−ρ‾i(t))∣. A_\pi(i,t)=\left|\frac{1}{N_y}\sum_{j=0}^{N_y-1}(-1)^j \bigl(\rho_{i,j}(t)-\overline\rho_i(t)\bigr)\right|. Aπ​(i,t)=​Ny​1​j=0∑Ny​−1​(−1)j(ρi,j​(t)−ρ​i​(t))​.

Record its time history and the maximum over the shock neighborhood, together with shock position, transverse velocity, pressure, and positivity. For a moving shock, track the shock neighborhood rather than a single fixed column. Other wavelengths need their own diagnostics. A small final residual or a visually smooth contour is insufficient evidence.

Status in this edition#

The Double Mach Reflection exhibit is an actual first-order HLL computation of an oblique shock interaction. It is not a controlled Roe-versus-HLL carbuncle experiment and supplies no carbuncle-free certification. The planar-shock section below adds a controlled row-perturbation diagnostic; a separate stage adds conforming-grid cylinder-forebody snapshots and controls. The physical cylindrical viscous stress and numerical shock dissipation also represent different operators.

Continue with Roe’s legacy, the flux benchmarks, and the implementation roadmap.

Computed planar odd–even diagnostic#

Open the controlled comparison. This independent test uses a stationary Mach-6 normal shock in [0,1] × [0,0.25], γ=1.4, upstream (ρ,u,v,p)=(1.4,6,0,1), and exact normal-shock downstream states. Both x boundaries are fixed, y is periodic, and cells are square. Compare 64 × 16 and 128 × 32 at t=0.2 using first-order space, SSPRK2 and CFL 0.3. The shock is either at x=0.5, aligned with a face, or half a cell farther right. Initial conservative means integrate a row-dependent front displacement of ±10⁻⁴Δx exactly. Each configuration has an unperturbed control.

Compare raw Roe, Roe with acoustic smoothing δ=0.1c̃, Davis HLL, Einfeldt-type HLLE, a pressure-sensor Roe/HLLE blend, and the common-sound-speed cubic-pressure AUSM baseline. All runs use the same spatial/time settings; their step counts and costs need not match. The blend uses S=max_neighbors |p_neighbor−p|/min(p_neighbor,p), θ=clip((S−0.05)/0.2,0,1), and the maximum adjacent cell θ at each face. F=(1−θ)F_Roe_fixed+θF_HLLE. The x-pressure jump can therefore activate HLLE on nearby transverse faces. This is an explicit educational sensor, not the published rotated-hybrid construction or a universal cure.

Measure max_i Aπ over |x−xshock|<0.1, pressure/density admissibility, retry counts, transverse velocity and each row's integrated mass-deficit position. The latter is not a pointwise detected front location. Density maps subtract the transverse row mean, using one signed color range per comparison. The history's logarithmic display floors values at 10⁻¹⁶; raw values remain in the download. No state clipping or hidden flux replacement is used.

Face-aligned Roe runs amplify the chosen row mode; shifting the shock half a cell changes the response substantially. The entropy correction does not remove this position sensitivity. HLL/HLLE and the other fluxes must be judged from these stated runs, rather than their names. The special Nyquist seed preserves a symmetry with zero transverse velocity even as density rows separate, so this experiment does not probe general transverse motion.

Reproduce with python scripts/build_shock_robustness.py. Download all perturbed/control histories, definitions and source hashes and final conservative fields. This is not the original Quirk moving-shock/perturbed-grid duct or a blunt-body carbuncle bulge. Cylinder-forebody cases are now a separate computed stage. Other wavelengths, mesh rotations and broader CFL/strength sweeps remain required work; no carbuncle-free claim is made. See Property U for the separate single-jump algebra.

Rotated Riemann sources: Ren (2003), Roe–Nishikawa et al. (2005), Nishikawa–Kitamura (2008) and the atlas experiment

chapman-enskog.title: Chapman–Enskog expansion: from populations to transport
chapman-enskog.html:
Chapman–Enskog expansion: from populations to transport

Chapman–Enskog（チャップマン–エンスコッグ）expansion separates kinetic relaxation from slowly varying hydrodynamic fields. The classical kinetic theory is treated by Chapman and Cowling's The Mathematical Theory of Non-Uniform Gases (first edition 1939; third edition 1970). The book's date is not the invention date of the expansion. This chapter gives an independent, unforced, isothermal lattice-BGK derivation at low Mach number.

A small parameter and solvability#

Introduce a bookkeeping parameter ε for slow variation:

fq=fq(0)+ϵfq(1)+ϵ2fq(2)+⋯ ,∂t=ϵ∂t1+ϵ2∂t2,∇=ϵ∇1. f_q=f_q^{(0)}+\epsilon f_q^{(1)}+\epsilon^2 f_q^{(2)}+\cdots, \quad \partial_t=\epsilon\partial_{t_1}+\epsilon^2\partial_{t_2}, \quad \nabla=\epsilon\nabla_1. fq​=fq(0)​+ϵfq(1)​+ϵ2fq(2)​+⋯,∂t​=ϵ∂t1​​+ϵ2∂t2​​,∇=ϵ∇1​.

Conserved moments are carried by the local equilibrium, so higher-order corrections have zero mass and momentum moments:

∑qfq(k)=0,∑qcqfq(k)=0(k≥1). \sum_q f_q^{(k)}=0,\quad \sum_q\boldsymbol c_q f_q^{(k)}=0\quad (k\geq1). q∑​fq(k)​=0,q∑​cq​fq(k)​=0(k≥1).

These are constraints on the expansion, not instructions to erase the nonequilibrium stress. The stress moment of f^(1) produces viscous transport.

Keep the discrete-time Taylor term#

For lattice BGK, expand the streaming side with D_q=∂t+c_q·∇. In lattice time units the Taylor series starts as D_q f_q + D_q² f_q/2. At successive orders,

fq(0)=fqeq,fq(1)=−τD1qfqeq, f_q^{(0)}=f_q^{eq},\qquad f_q^{(1)}=-\tau D_{1q} f_q^{eq}, fq(0)​=fqeq​,fq(1)​=−τD1q​fqeq​,
∂t2fqeq+(1−12τ)D1qfq(1)=−fq(2)τ. \partial_{t_2} f_q^{eq} +\left(1-\frac1{2\tau}\right)D_{1q}f_q^{(1)} =-\frac{f_q^{(2)}}{\tau}. ∂t2​​fqeq​+(1−2τ1​)D1q​fq(1)​=−τfq(2)​​.

The first-order mass and momentum moments give the continuity and Euler parts. The second-order stress correction supplies the Newtonian viscous part. D2Q9 equilibrium isotropy, the low-Mach approximation, and the preceding factor give the shear viscosity

ν=cs2(τ−12)Δt. \nu=c_s^2\left(\tau-\frac12\right)\Delta t. ν=cs2​(τ−21​)Δt.

Here τ is the dimensionless number of lattice time steps used for relaxation, with physical τ_relax=τΔt. Continuous-time BGK instead gives ν=c_s²τ_relax for the corresponding isothermal model; there is no streaming Taylor half-step in that continuous equation. Mixing those definitions yields a wrong viscosity.

What this derivation does and does not establish#

The D2Q9 experiment measures shear damping rather than only substituting this formula. Qian et al. (1992) is the lattice-model source; the BGK source concerns continuous kinetic relaxation. Guo et al. (2002) treats the force discretization separately; the unforced algebra above does not derive its source term.

This is a formal near-equilibrium asymptotic expansion, with small gradients and small Mach number for the truncated isothermal equilibrium. It does not prove stability near shocks, justify arbitrary relaxation times, recover an energy equation, or make this model a general rarefied-gas Boltzmann solver. Burnett-order transport and thermal collision models require additional moments and analysis.
