automatic-differentiation.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
automatic-differentiation.html:
Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers

Automatic differentiation (AD) evaluates derivatives by applying the chain rule to the elementary operations in a program. It supplies Jacobians for Newton iterations, directional derivatives for Krylov methods, and sensitivities for parameter estimation. These are shared numerical foundations across many physical models.

Implemented here: a small forward-mode dual-number engine and a comparison of analytic differentiation, finite differences and AD on the existing Bratu boundary-value problem. The experiment reuses the atlas's Armijo-damped Newton solver. Reverse mode, implicit sensitivities and adjoints are explained as connections; this exhibit does not implement them.

Four ways to obtain a derivative

An analytic derivative is derived mathematically and entered into the solver by hand. It can expose structure and provide an independent reference, but the derivative must be kept consistent with the residual implementation. Symbolic differentiation manipulates expressions into another expression. AD instead carries numerical derivative information through the evaluated operations, without constructing a global symbolic formula.

Finite differences estimate a derivative from perturbed function values. For a vector residual F and a direction v, forward and centered differences are

Dε+F(u)v=F(u+εv)−F(u)ε,Dε0F(u)v=F(u+εv)−F(u−εv)2ε.D_\varepsilon^+F(u)v=\frac{F(u+\varepsilon v)-F(u)}{\varepsilon}, \qquad D_\varepsilon^0F(u)v=\frac{F(u+\varepsilon v)-F(u-\varepsilon v)}{2\varepsilon}.Dε+​F(u)v=εF(u+εv)−F(u)​,Dε0​F(u)v=2εF(u+εv)−F(u−εv)​.

For sufficiently smooth F, their truncation errors are first and second order in ε. A very small ε amplifies cancellation and rounding in the residual evaluations. The useful step depends on the state, direction, precision and scaling of F. A finite-difference check should therefore sweep several steps.

AD has no finite-difference step or associated truncation error. It still uses floating-point arithmetic: unstable formulas, overflow, underflow and rounding can affect both values and derivatives. The differentiated object is the composition of real-arithmetic operations represented by the executed program, evaluated numerically. It is not the derivative of the discontinuous mapping from one set of floating-point bit patterns to another.

Forward mode: carry a value and a direction

Seed the input with a direction v and propagate pairs consisting of a value and its directional derivative. Dual-number notation makes the chain rule visible:

a^=a+ηa˙,η2=0,a^b^=ab+η(a˙b+ab˙),exp⁡(a^)=exp⁡(a)+ηexp⁡(a)a˙.\widehat a=a+\eta\dot a,\qquad \eta^2=0, \qquad \widehat a\widehat b=ab+\eta(\dot a b+a\dot b), \qquad \exp(\widehat a)=\exp(a)+\eta\exp(a)\dot a.a=a+ηa˙,η2=0,ab=ab+η(a˙b+ab˙),exp(a)=exp(a)+ηexp(a)a˙.

The nilpotent symbol η is an algebraic device, not a small numerical step. The implementation stores the two arrays separately. It overloads the small set of operations needed for this experiment, including elementwise arithmetic, indexing, exponentiation and multiplication by a constant matrix. Unsupported operations are outside this educational engine's scope.

For F from n inputs to m outputs, one seeded execution returns F(u) and J(u)v. This Jacobian–vector product (JVP) avoids storing an m-by-n Jacobian. Seed each coordinate basis vector in turn to assemble all n columns. The Bratu comparison deliberately uses that transparent assembly; it does not exploit sparsity coloring or provide a matrix-free Newton solver.

Reverse mode and the derivative you actually need

Reverse mode propagates an output weight w backwards through local derivative rules to obtain J(u)ᵀw, often called a vector–Jacobian product (VJP). For a scalar objective with many parameters, one reverse pass can produce its gradient. An implementation commonly retains intermediate values or recomputes them through checkpointing. Forward mode is attractive when only a few input directions are required. The relevant dimensions are the numbers of independent inputs and outputs, together with the requested products.

A Hessian–vector product for a smooth scalar objective can be obtained by differentiating its gradient in a direction. Explicitly assembling a Hessian is unnecessary when an optimization method only needs that product. See Baydin et al. (2018) for an AD survey and the JAX autodiff cookbook for practical JVP, VJP and higher-order constructions. JAX is a reading reference; the local experiment requires only the atlas's existing NumPy environment.

The existing Bratu problem

We retain the same sign convention, parameter and exact solution used in the sparse and nonlinear systems verification:

−u′′(x)−λeu(x)=0,0<x<1,u(0)=u(1)=0,λ=2cosh⁡2(1/2),-u''(x)-\lambda e^{u(x)}=0,\qquad 0<x<1,\qquad u(0)=u(1)=0, \qquad \lambda=\frac{2}{\cosh^2(1/2)},−u′′(x)−λeu(x)=0,0<x<1,u(0)=u(1)=0,λ=cosh2(1/2)2​,
u∗(x)=−2log⁡ ⁣(cosh⁡(x−1/2)cosh⁡(1/2)).u_*(x)=-2\log\!\left(\frac{\cosh(x-1/2)}{\cosh(1/2)}\right).u∗​(x)=−2log(cosh(1/2)cosh(x−1/2)​).

Here n denotes the number of interior unknowns. The interval has n+1 uniform cells, with h=1/(n+1) and nodes x_i=ih. Centered differences give

Fi(u)=2ui−ui−1−ui+1h2−λeui,u0=un+1=0,F_i(u)=\frac{2u_i-u_{i-1}-u_{i+1}}{h^2}-\lambda e^{u_i}, \qquad u_0=u_{n+1}=0,Fi​(u)=h22ui​−ui−1​−ui+1​​−λeui​,u0​=un+1​=0,
J(u)=D−λdiag⁡(eu),D=1h2tridiag⁡(−1,2,−1).J(u)=D-\lambda\operatorname{diag}(e^u), \qquad D=\frac{1}{h^2}\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1).J(u)=D−λdiag(eu),D=h21​tridiag(−1,2,−1).

The analytic Jacobian is an independent formula. Finite differences and AD both evaluate the same residual function. In particular, AD differentiates the discrete residual F; it does not remove the centered stencil's spatial discretization error. The exact continuous solution is used to check spatial refinement, not as an exact root of the discrete equations.

Verification: hold the problem fixed

The saved measurements and source hashes separate three checks so that accurate derivatives and accurate PDE solutions are not confused.

The derivative check uses n=31 and the state u_*(x_i)+0.05 sin(3πx_i), away from the exact continuous profile. Its direction is sin(2πx_i)+0.3 cos(5πx_i), normalized to unit Euclidean length. The sweep contains 29 logarithmically spaced, absolute perturbations from 1 down to 10⁻¹⁴; these are derivative perturbations, not spatial mesh widths.

  1. Differentiate at a fixed state. Compare the assembled forward-mode AD Jacobian and its JVP against the analytic formula. Sweep finite-difference steps at that same state, using both forward and centered differences. Report relative Frobenius errors for matrices and relative Euclidean errors for directional products. A deterministic smooth direction prevents run-to-run changes in the comparison.
  2. Solve the same discrete system. Start every Newton solve at zero, use the same residual, Armijo search, dense linear solve and residual tolerance, and change only how the Jacobian is supplied. The finite-difference run uses a fixed centered-difference step recorded in the manifest. Measure the true residual after each accepted iteration and compare the final roots with the analytic-Jacobian solve.
  3. Refine the mesh. Repeat the three methods for n=15, 31 and 63 interior nodes. Compare their roots with u_* at the interior nodes using a nodal maximum error. Approximately fourfold error reduction under halving h identifies the centered scheme's second-order spatial behavior.

In the saved run, AD and the analytic Jacobian agree entry by entry, while the relative JVP error is about 8×10⁻¹⁶. This exact matrix agreement is specific to the operation ordering in this example, not a general guarantee of bitwise agreement for AD. The finite-difference curves show the useful range between truncation error and cancellation. All nine Newton solves reach the common absolute residual Euclidean tolerance 10⁻¹⁰ in three updates. The fixed centered-difference perturbation is 10⁻⁵; its final roots agree with the analytic-Jacobian roots to less than 10⁻¹⁴ in nodal maximum norm. The continuous nodal maximum errors are approximately 1.738×10⁻⁴, 4.337×10⁻⁵ and 1.084×10⁻⁵ on the three grids. Their factor-of-four reduction remains after changing the derivative calculation: spatial discretization sets the leading solution error here.

The matrix norm includes entries of size h⁻². A small relative matrix error can therefore hide errors in smaller terms. The direct directional check is reported separately, rather than relying only on a product of the assembled finite-difference matrix.

The analytic derivative is a reference, not an assumption that every analytic implementation is correct. The tests also check derivative rules on separate functions and nontrivial directions, and check Bratu refinement against the continuous solution. Agreement between two Jacobians alone would not validate the boundary conditions or the PDE discretization.

The figure makes no speed ranking. Assembling a dense AD Jacobian here needs n forward seeds; centered differences need two residual evaluations per column. Counts describe these implementations, not equal-cost operations or the best sparse AD strategy. For a large Newton–Krylov method, supplying Jv directly can be preferable to constructing every column, while a suitable preconditioner remains necessary.

Connections to implicit integration and parameter estimation

An implicit ODE stage has a residual involving the state and time step. Its Newton matrix contains derivatives of the ODE right-hand side, so the same AD construction can supply them. For parameter estimation, derivatives of observations or an objective with respect to model parameters connect a simulation to an optimization method. Derivative availability does not itself choose a stable integrator, a well-conditioned parameterization or a convergent optimization algorithm.

Suppose the converged discrete state satisfies F(u,θ)=0. At a differentiable solution with nonsingular F_u, its parameter sensitivity satisfies

Fududθ=−Fθ.F_u\frac{du}{d\theta}=-F_\theta.Fu​dθdu​=−Fθ​.

For a scalar objective L(u,θ), an adjoint solve gives

FuTp=LuT,dLdθ=Lθ−pTFθ.F_u^T p=L_u^T,\qquad \frac{dL}{d\theta}=L_\theta-p^TF_\theta.FuT​p=LuT​,dθdL​=Lθ​−pTFθ​.

This differentiates the equation defining the solution. Differentiating a fixed, finite sequence of Newton iterations instead gives the derivative of that sequence, including its dependence on the initial guess. Stopping criteria and line-search branches complicate that distinction. Near a singular Jacobian, sensitivities can be large even when the primal residual is small. Primal and derivative solve tolerances therefore need separate checks. These sensitivity and adjoint equations are explanatory extensions; the present Bratu exhibit compares Jacobians used in the primal solve.

Limits: smoothness, branches and numerical stability

AD applies the derivative rules of the operations that are executed. At a branch boundary, an absolute-value corner or a limiter switch, the underlying function may have no unique classical derivative; a library's chosen rule does not establish one. Adaptive time-step decisions can change the executed path under parameter perturbations. For shocks, a computed grid-value derivative also needs interpretation in terms of shock motion and the quantity being measured.

The discretized derivative should be checked for mesh and time-step convergence when it is intended to approximate a continuous sensitivity. Differentiating a discretized solver and discretizing continuous sensitivity or adjoint equations require their own consistency analysis. Stable function evaluation matters too: a formula that overflows in the primal calculation is not repaired by applying the chain rule.

Reproduce the comparison

Extract the November 22, 2026 release ZIP into a new folder. Prepare a Python environment with NumPy, Matplotlib and pytest, and run from the extracted folder. See the README for the complete instructions.

python -m pip install numpy matplotlib pytest
python scripts/build_autodiff.py
python -m pytest tests/test_autodiff.py

Read the AD engine and Bratu residual, existing Newton solver, figure and evidence builder, and test source individually. An independent-extraction verification record and source inventory and hashes accompany the package.

The builder writes the figure and a JSON manifest containing grids, parameters, finite-difference steps, stopping controls, norms, solver histories, the numerical environment and source SHA-256 hashes. Evidence is generated from the numerical implementation independently of the website build. The dated supplement includes the forward-mode engine, Bratu comparison, tests and saved results introduced here. Reverse-mode and adjoint solvers remain outside this implementation. Continue with Newton and conditioning, stiff integration, or the error-norm guide.

Implicit differentiation and adjoints: verified Bratu sensitivity

Executable implicit state sensitivities and discrete adjoints are now provided in the separate Bratu parameter-sensitivity chapter. This does not expand the earlier forward-mode release; a separate dated supplement checks root sensitivity and total objective derivatives.

Publication scope and related entries

A separate November 22, 2026 supplement fixes its source, tests, figure and JSON evidence. Reverse mode, Hessian-vector products, implicit sensitivities and adjoints are reading connections rather than implemented solvers in this exhibit. pinn-operators.title: PINNs and neural operators
pinn-operators.html:
PINNs and neural operators

A PINN fits a neural representation of a particular solution; a neural operator learns a map from input functions such as coefficients or initial data to solution functions. Their targets and validation protocols differ.

Problem and representative equations

A PINN minimizes an empirical weighted loss of PDE, boundary and data residuals. N and B are differential/boundary operators and f,g are prescribed data. A representative FNO layer combines a Fourier-parameterized integral operator K with a local map W acting on feature functions v.

L(θ)=λr⟨∣N[uθ]−f∣2⟩r+λb⟨∣B[uθ]−g∣2⟩b+λd⟨∣uθ−uobs∣2⟩d.\mathcal L(\theta)=\lambda_r\langle|\mathcal N[u_\theta]-f|^2\rangle_r+\lambda_b\langle|\mathcal B[u_\theta]-g|^2\rangle_b+\lambda_d\langle|u_\theta-u_{\rm obs}|^2\rangle_d.L(θ)=λr​⟨∣N[uθ​]−f∣2⟩r​+λb​⟨∣B[uθ​]−g∣2⟩b​+λd​⟨∣uθ​−uobs​∣2⟩d​.
vℓ+1=σ ⁣(Wℓvℓ+F−1[Kℓ Fvℓ]).v_{\ell+1}=\sigma\!\left(W_\ell v_\ell+\mathcal F^{-1}[K_\ell\,\mathcal Fv_\ell]\right).vℓ+1​=σ(Wℓ​vℓ​+F−1[Kℓ​Fvℓ​]).

Algorithm

For a PINN, scale coordinates/units, differentiate residuals, specify collocation points and boundary enforcement, and optimize. FNO trains an operator on input/reference-solution pairs and truncates Fourier modes. Cite the PINN and FNO papers as separate proposals.

Conditions and pitfalls

Small training loss is not a bound on global solution error or conservation. Examine residual imbalance, shocks, stiff scales and out-of-distribution inputs. Transfer between discretizations is not a guarantee of physical correctness at arbitrary resolution.

What to check

Compare against analytic or independently converged conventional solutions. Measure off-training L1/L2/L∞ errors, boundaries, conservation and multiple seeds. Split operator data by independent problems rather than nearby time slices alone, and report distribution-shift tests separately.

Publication scope and related entries

rotated-hybrid.title: Rotated-hybrid Riemann solver
rotated-hybrid.html:
Rotated-hybrid Riemann solver

Rotated Riemann methods construct dissipation using directions beyond the face normal. Ren’s rotated Roe method (2003) and Nishikawa–Kitamura’s rotated-hybrid method (2008) are related but distinct.

Problem and representative equations

For 2D Euler states U_L,U_R and unit face normal n, resolve n into orthogonal unit directions n₁,n₂ with weights αᵢ=n·nᵢ. The formula below defines this atlas’s educational HLLE/Roe experiment, not the optimized dissipation formula in the 2008 paper.

n=α1n1+α2n2,F^(n)=α1F^HLLE(n1)+α2F^Roe(n2).\mathbf n=\alpha_1\mathbf n_1+\alpha_2\mathbf n_2,\qquad\widehat F(\mathbf n)=\alpha_1\widehat F_{\rm HLLE}(\mathbf n_1)+\alpha_2\widehat F_{\rm Roe}(\mathbf n_2).n=α1​n1​+α2​n2​,F(n)=α1​FHLLE​(n1​)+α2​FRoe​(n2​).

Algorithm

The implementation aligns n₁ with the velocity jump, orienting directions to have nonnegative projections on the face normal. A tiny jump falls back to the face tangent. Rotate the same states into each frame, evaluate HLLE/Roe, rotate momentum fluxes back and combine. This differs from a pressure-sensor flux blend.

Conditions and pitfalls

Roe (1981) supplies the component approximate solver. The 2003 rotated-method paper is by Y.-X. Ren; the 2008 rotated-hybrid paper is by Hiroaki Nishikawa and Keiichi Kitamura. Roe, Nishikawa, Ismail and Scalabrin (2005) is related carbuncle research, not the authorship/date of that 2008 paper. No universal carbuncle or positivity guarantee is claimed here.

What to check

Check constant states, flux reversal under state/normal exchange and rotational covariance. Separate normal compression from pure tangential shear, then compare perturbed planar shocks and blunt-body cases under fixed conditions. Link the dated package’s actual tests/results without claiming a new reproduction of the papers.

Publication scope and related entries

low-mach-preconditioning.html:
Preconditioning matrices, low Mach numbers, sonic points and entropy fixes

Separate acoustic/convective preconditioning from transonic numerical-viscosity corrections. Connect a concrete Γ, a linear eigenvalue model, Mach cutoffs and dual time stepping with explicit variable conventions.

Matrix-solve and PDE preconditioning

Left preconditioning P⁻¹Ax=P⁻¹b assists an iterative linear solve. Low-Mach PDE preconditioning instead changes pseudo-time mass matrices or characteristic numerical dissipation. Papers may use P for both; identify the operator being modified first.

At low Mach number, |u_n±a| is large compared with convection |u_n|, affecting steady iteration and low-speed flux accuracy. This is a different limit from a transonic characteristic u_n±a=0.

Place Γ on pseudo time

Distinguish conservative U from primitive q and pseudo time τ from physical time t. Steady problems omit the physical-time term. Unsteady dual-time iterations retain the physically discretized term, such as BDF2, throughout the inner solve. Γ is not the same matrix as U_q.

For nonsingular Γ and unchanged R, a converged steady pseudo-time solve still satisfies R=0. Preconditioning spatial dissipation additionally changes the discrete residual construction. Indiscriminately preconditioning physical time changes the unsteady solution, including acoustics.

Γ(q)∂q∂τ+∂U(q)∂t+R(U(q))=0,q=(p,u,v,w,T)T.\Gamma(q)\frac{\partial q}{\partial\tau}+\frac{\partial U(q)}{\partial t}+R(U(q))=0,\qquad q=(p,u,v,w,T)^T.Γ(q)∂τ∂q​+∂t∂U(q)​+R(U(q))=0,q=(p,u,v,w,T)T.

A concrete Weiss–Smith-type matrix

For a calorically perfect ideal gas, use q=(p,u,v,w,T), total specific enthalpy H=c_pT+(u²+v²+w²)/2, constant c_p, ρ_T=(∂ρ/∂T)_p and physical sound speed a. Θ replaces the usual pressure-density derivative. This ideal-gas specialization is not a general real-fluid formula.

Setting U_ref=a gives Θ=ρ/p and recovers the physical Jacobian U_q in this ordering. Reducing U_ref toward a convective scale changes pseudo-acoustic scales. Γ, its inverse and a conservative-variable P are not numerically identical matrices.

Stagnation singularities and a Mach cutoff

A representative bounded parameter is shown below. Positive M_cut prevents U_ref=0 at stagnation; the upper bound recovers the physical system at supersonic speed. This is an illustrative choice, not a universal prescription: viscous, unsteady and boundary-aware variants use other reference scales.

The cutoff avoids degeneracy of the preconditioner near zero velocity; it does not remove physical Mach-1 flow from the domain. Too large a cutoff weakens low-Mach benefits; too small a value can impair robustness or boundary behavior.

How characteristic eigenvalues change

To expose the effect, linearize about constant density/sound speed and use pressure perturbation divided by ρ₀a, normal/tangential velocities and an advected entropy variable with fixed scaling. The following P is an illustrative pressure-row scaling, not the nonlinear Γ above.

Preconditioning does not remove a physical sonic zero

The model has zero acoustic eigenvalue product when u_n²=a². More generally, multiplication by an invertible P cannot remove singularity of A. Do not claim that a preconditioning matrix eliminates physical sonic points. Sonic singularities of particular attempts at isotropic acoustic preconditioning also require formulation-specific discussion.

Transonic rarefaction and an entropy fix

A Roe linearization can produce an unphysical expansion shock when a characteristic crosses zero through a rarefaction. A representative smoothing replaces |λ| in the numerical dissipation as below. δ has speed units; state-aware choices and fixed fractional cutoffs are different variants.

This modifies numerical viscosity rather than deleting the physical characteristic. The published acoustic quadratic smoothing is not claimed as a faithful reproduction of every Harten–Hyman construction. Entropy correction, HLLE low-density robustness, carbuncle control and low-Mach preconditioning address different problems.

Checks that keep the mechanisms separate

Test spectra, recovery at β→1, low-Mach scaling and near-stagnation invertibility on small linear problems. Measure pseudo-time convergence separately from solution error due to changed spatial fluxes. Interior eigenvalue analysis alone cannot assess boundary reflection.

Use transonic Burgers/Euler rarefactions to examine expansion shocks, refinement and δ sensitivity. For unsteady problems separate physical-time convergence from inner pseudo-residual convergence. Low-Mach checks here are proposed work; existing Jacobi scaling or dual-time examples do not validate a dedicated low-Mach flow solver.

steady-runge-kutta.title: Damping Runge–Kutta iterations for steady solutions
steady-runge-kutta.html:
Damping Runge–Kutta iterations for steady solutions

Interpret multistage pseudo-time iterations as smoothers for a steady residual. A Jameson–Schmidt–Turkel-family example connects stage coefficients, stability polynomials, nonlinear order, high-frequency damping and preconditioning.

The target is R(U)=0, not a physical-time trajectory

For a discrete steady Euler/Navier–Stokes residual R, iterate an artificial ODE in pseudo time τ toward its root. Here R is the conservative residual divided by cell volume. The step is a pseudo-time step; the aim is an adequately converged residual and steady observables, not an accurate physical transient.

The following base-state recurrence forms every stage from the same U^(0), unlike chaining forward-Euler increments from the preceding stage. Compare coefficients only after matching residual sign, cell-volume scaling and any preconditioning action.

dUdτ=−R(U),U(0)=Un,U(k)=U(0)−αkΔτR(U(k−1)),Un+1=U(s).\frac{dU}{d\tau}=-R(U),\quad U^{(0)}=U^n,\quad U^{(k)}=U^{(0)}-\alpha_k\Delta\tau R(U^{(k-1)}),\quad U^{n+1}=U^{(s)}.dτdU​=−R(U),U(0)=Un,U(k)=U(0)−αk​ΔτR(U(k−1)),Un+1=U(s).

A representative Jameson-family four-stage iteration

Consider these coefficients with the same autonomous residual reevaluated at every stage. For R(U)=AU, the stability polynomial equals classical RK4. The simplified recurrence is not a complete specification of the original fluxes, artificial dissipation and dissipation-update schedule.

Equality of linear stability polynomials does not establish nonlinear fourth-order physical-time accuracy. This base-state recurrence is generally second order for nonlinear autonomous ODEs: it fails the third-order condition bᵀ(c⊙c)=1/3. Distinguish its steady-solver purpose and nonlinear order conditions from classical RK4.

(α1,α2,α3,α4)=(1/4,1/3,1/2,1),z=−Δτλ,R4(z)=1+z+z2/2+z3/6+z4/24.(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\alpha_4)=(1/4,1/3,1/2,1),\qquad z=-\Delta\tau\lambda,\quad \mathcal R_4(z)=1+z+z^2/2+z^3/6+z^4/24.(α1​,α2​,α3​,α4​)=(1/4,1/3,1/2,1),z=−Δτλ,R4​(z)=1+z+z2/2+z3/6+z4/24.
bTc=12,bT(c⊙c)=14≠13for the stated base-state four-stage recurrence.b^Tc=\tfrac12,\qquad b^T(c\odot c)=\tfrac14\ne\tfrac13\quad\text{for the stated base-state four-stage recurrence}.bTc=21​,bT(c⊙c)=41​=31​for the stated base-state four-stage recurrence.

Stability and high-frequency damping are different

For linearized residual modes, the iteration multiplier is a stability polynomial. |ℛ|≤1 prevents growth, but |ℛ| near one barely damps error. A multigrid smoother seeks small maximum amplification μ on frequencies H not representable on the coarse grid.

For a purely decaying z=−2 mode, this four-stage polynomial gives ℛ=1/3, while near-zero low-frequency modes decay slowly. Pushing the step to a stability boundary does not maximize damping or minimize time to convergence. Advection and diffusion occupy different spectral regions.

Residual smoothing, preconditioning and multigrid

Residual smoothing is a separate spatial filtering operation, not the choice of RK stage coefficients. With dimensionless centered D₂ on a uniform periodic grid and ε≥0, the example below attenuates high-frequency residuals. An invertible filter retains the residual root but changes the iteration spectrum.

Low-Mach preconditioning changes acoustic/convective scales, local stepping changes per-cell iteration increments, and coarse correction treats errors poorly reduced by the smoother. Combined iterations still require boundary/variable-coefficient/nonnormality analysis and must be distinguished from physical-time integration.

Measure Fourier-mode damping on a manufactured Poisson-type problem and compare with μ. For compressible flow track true residuals scaled by conservative component and steady quantities such as forces, mass flow and conservation balances. When smoothing residuals, also display the original unsmoothed residual.

Report residual evaluations and linear-solve work, final errors and termination reasons, not only stage/cycle counts. Compare methods at the same steady solution and tolerance. This chapter supplies algorithmic reading, not a dedicated Jameson solver or new flow-validation results.

h2-hf.title: Closed-shell HF for H₂: independent references, SCF residuals and basis refinement
h2-hf.html:
Closed-shell HF for H₂: independent references, SCF residuals and basis refinement

Solve two-electron H₂ at fixed proton positions using original s-Gaussian integrals and restricted closed-shell Hartree–Fock (RHF). Energy stabilization, satisfaction of the discrete SCF equations, changes under basis expansion and physical accuracy are separate questions.

This implementation covers isolated two-electron H2 RHF in finite s-only bases. It does not implement general molecular HF, establish a complete-basis limit, recover the correlated dissociation curve, or supply molecular/periodic DFT.

Fixed input, code, tests and acceptance · ZIP · Independent-extraction verification / JSON

The model being solved

This is a Born–Oppenheimer electronic problem with the internuclear distance R fixed by the input. Atomic units are used: distances in bohr and energies in hartree. Relativistic effects, nuclear motion, vibration/rotation, solvent and periodic boundaries are excluded. Total energy including nuclear repulsion 1/R is recorded separately from electronic energy.

The two electrons occupy the same spatial orbital with opposite spins in closed-shell RHF. The same restriction is retained at stretched geometries. SCF convergence and agreement with another implementation do not establish the correct dissociation limit or recover electron correlation. This is not a switch to UHF, configuration interaction or DFT.

Gaussian basis functions and original integrals

Normalized s-type Gaussians centered on the two nuclei form the basis. A contracted function combines several exponents and coefficients, with normalization also applied to the contraction. Three primitives in STO-3G describe one contracted s function, not three independent basis functions. Inputs and results retain exponents, coefficients and contractions. The STO-3G numerical convention is checked against Basis Set Exchange version 1, rather than presented as a direct transcription of the original paper’s printed digits.

The educational code computes overlap S, kinetic T, nuclear attraction V and electron-repulsion integrals, defining the one-electron matrix as h=T+V. The s-type Coulomb integrals involve the Boys function F₀, which tends to 1 as t approaches zero. Direct evaluation of erf(√t)/√t at zero would produce 0/0, so the limiting region needs a stable treatment. The chemists’ integral index convention and spin-summed density P determine the factor 1/2 in exchange.

How SCF convergence is judged

Symmetric orthogonalization converts the Roothaan equation to an ordinary eigenproblem. Occupied orbitals define a new density, which rebuilds the Fock matrix for the next iteration. Density mixing can stabilize iterations, but an intermediate mixed density need not satisfy the idempotency condition of a pure determinant. Final density, orbitals and Fock matrix are therefore checked in a consistent state.

A small energy change alone is insufficient. Energy change, the Frobenius norm of the AO-density change and the Frobenius norm of the orthonormal-coordinate commutator residual are compared with input thresholds. Orbital orthogonality, electron count Tr(PS)=2 and closed-shell idempotency PSP=2P are also measured. The matrix-trace energy with F[P] rebuilt from the final density is compared with a separate occupied-orbital/electron-repulsion-integral reconstruction.

The minimum overlap eigenvalue and condition number are recorded. Near-linear dependence makes S⁻¹ᐟ² amplify errors. Termination reasons and iteration limits are explicit; reaching the limit is not reported as convergence. A stationary solution also need not be a stable minimum, so residual checks do not replace a full RHF/UHF stability analysis.

Basis refinement and its limits

SCF tolerance controls the remaining solution error within one fixed basis. A basis change changes the discrete problem itself. Basis comparisons retain tight SCF settings, geometry, nuclear repulsion and the RHF constraint. True RHF minima in nested variational spaces cannot increase in energy under expansion. Switching to a different local stationary branch would invalidate that simple comparison.

Refinement here is limited to the finite s-only sequence defined by the public input. Adjacent-basis energy changes are measured, but the absence of p and higher angular functions means this does not prove convergence to the complete-basis-set (CBS) limit or chemical accuracy. Unrelated basis sets and different contractions are not all treated as a nested sequence. For each separation, the final two additions are checked against the stated energy-change target. This is a stopping diagnostic for the published sequence, not an upper bound on true basis error.

The tolerance sweep changes only SCF thresholds and compares with a tighter solution. The basis sweep keeps SCF settings aligned. These differences and independent-implementation differences are separate outputs. A small final basis increment does not eliminate physical approximation error.

Independent reference and reproduction

The reference script supplies the same geometry, charge, spin and explicit Gaussian basis to PySCF, using its independent integral library and SCF procedure for RHF energies. It does not call the educational integral, Fock or SCF functions. Both calculations solve the same physical model in the same finite basis; the comparison is not against an exact correlated energy.

The release records input/reference hashes, dependency versions, total energies, reference differences, iteration histories and termination reasons. Extract the ZIP into another directory and run the same fixed input, checking residual/error values against criteria as well as the JSON pass flag. Regenerating the independent reference is separate from ordinary reruns using the saved reference.

Sources: Qiming Sun et al. (2020), PySCF developers (2026)

periodic-dft.html:
Periodic DFT: Γ points, k-point integration, basis sets, SCF and an independent reference

A small periodic cell containing one He atom connects Bloch’s theorem, k-point integration, periodic Gaussian bases, auxiliary FFT grids and SCF iteration. A PySCF-backed example is compared with an independent plane-wave DFTK reference, exposing the conventions needed to solve the same model with different discretizations.

This educational periodic problem uses nonrelativistic, spin-unpolarized LDA for a fixed simple-cubic He cell. The implementation is a driver using PySCF, rather than a DFT engine written from scratch. It does not optimize crystal structure or predict equilibrium solid helium.

The fixed physical model and the numerical errors being tested

The input is a simple-cubic cell of side 4 bohr containing one He atom at the origin. A local GTH–PADE pseudopotential supplies two valence electrons for a closed-shell, spin-unpolarized Kohn–Sham problem. This He potential has no nonlocal projectors. One example therefore does not validate general multielement crystals or nonlocal pseudopotentials. The geometry is fixed as a teaching configuration for convergence experiments.

The exchange-correlation functional is specified explicitly as Libxc LDA_X plus LDA_C_VWN (VWN5). The label LDA alone does not align choices such as VWN and Perdew–Wang correlation. GTH–PADE names the chosen pseudopotential; it does not assert that its generation approximation is identical to the VWN5 used here. Both engines receive the same pseudopotential coefficients and exchange-correlation choice.

Atomic units are used, with lattice lengths in bohr and energies in hartree. Total energies are compared per unit cell, including electronic terms and periodic ion–ion interactions. SCF solution error, k-point quadrature, the orbital basis and the auxiliary density/potential grid are varied separately. Reducing these numerical effects does not measure the physical error of LDA or the pseudopotential approximation.

Bloch’s theorem and the units of a k point

For a periodic potential, an orbital can be written as a plane-wave phase times a lattice-periodic function. The periodic function u and the Bloch orbital ψ are distinct: u is periodic across cell boundaries, whereas ψ satisfies a k-dependent phase boundary condition. Γ is the special point k=0, where this phase is one.

Here A contains direct lattice vectors as columns and B contains reciprocal vectors as columns, with AᵀB=2πI. Fractional coordinates κ give the physical wavevector k=Bκ. The coordinates κ are dimensionless; k is in bohr⁻¹ when the lattice is in bohr. PySCF stores cell vectors as rows and passes physical wavevectors to SCF. A shared input lattice and fractional k-point list prevent confusion with DFTK’s column convention.

Γ points and k meshes: quadrature versus band paths

Densities and energies of an infinite crystal involve integrals over the Brillouin zone. A finite set of k points and weights approximates these integrals. This example explicitly lists all points of a uniform mesh containing Γ and equal weights summing to one. Γ is included even for even subdivisions. This convention is not automatically identical to software defaults or the half-grid displacement of an even Monkhorst–Pack mesh. Fractional k points differing by an integer reciprocal vector represent the same point.

A Γ-only calculation is a one-point quadrature of the Brillouin zone. It can be adequate for some large real-space cells or localized orbitals, but adequacy for this small cell must be measured. Γ-only and several meshes are compared with the same orbital basis, auxiliary grid and SCF settings. Different meshes need not be nested, and monotonically decreasing energy differences are not assumed.

A band path joins high-symmetry points to visualize dispersion. Giving its points equal weights generally does not produce a Brillouin-zone quadrature. This example tests integrated energy and density; drawing a band path does not replace k-point convergence.

The orbital basis and auxiliary FFT grid are separate convergence axes

The PySCF orbitals expand Bloch sums of Gaussian functions. Results retain basis names such as gth-dzv, the actual function count and overlap conditioning. Increasing a basis’s zeta label does not prove a complete-basis limit; bases with different contractions and polarization functions are not necessarily mathematically nested. Basis differences measure sensitivity within the published finite sequence.

FFT density fitting (FFTDF) is an auxiliary plane-wave/FFT representation used for quantities such as density and Coulomb potentials. Refining its mesh does not enlarge the Gaussian orbital space. Conversely, enlarging only the orbital basis cannot remove errors from a coarse auxiliary grid. The PySCF auxiliary grid, DFTK orbital plane-wave cutoff and its associated density grid are distinct, and hartree must not be confused with rydberg.

The periodic Coulomb G=0 component is handled with a convention combining electrons, the local pseudopotential and periodic ionic terms. A change in the mean potential also shifts the orbital eigenvalue origin. Even the same physical model needs aligned G=0 constants, pseudopotential corrections, Ewald terms and per-cell versus per-atom units for direct total-energy comparison. Conventions and energy components are checked rather than adding an empirical constant to force agreement.

SCF residuals, electron count and a sampled KS gap

The Kohn–Sham potential depends on density, so an eigenproblem and density update are iterated. Energy changes are supplemented by a commutator residual built from the final density, orbital-equation residuals, orthogonality and electron count. The commutator measure is the maximum over k points of the Frobenius norm of X(FPS−SPF)X, with symmetric orthogonalization X=S⁻¹ᐟ². Orbital residuals use the same final-density F. Results retain iteration histories, stopping reasons and tolerances. Reaching an iteration cap is not labeled convergence.

A tolerance sweep changes only SCF settings at fixed discretization and measures the energy difference from a tight solution. This checks the remaining nonlinear solution error. SCF convergence is separate from sufficient orbital bases, auxiliary grids and k points, and from physical-model accuracy.

For closed-shell occupations, a sampled KS gap is obtained from the largest occupied and smallest unoccupied eigenvalues over all calculated k points. A positive value indicates separated occupations on that mesh. It neither guarantees the true minimum over the full Brillouin zone nor equals the many-body fundamental gap defined by adding/removing an electron or an experimental optical gap. Unoccupied states also depend on the orbital basis. A visible difference remains between the Gaussian and plane-wave sampled gaps in this example. The independent comparison validates total energies; gap convergence or agreement is not established.

Comparison with an independent DFTK reference in a different basis

The example uses PySCF’s periodic integrals, FFTDF and SCF. The independent Julia package DFTK supplies a plane-wave Kohn–Sham reference without calling the teaching PySCF solver. Merely changing an auxiliary representation within PySCF would not be an independent-implementation comparison. Both engines use Libxc for exchange-correlation evaluation, so that component is not independently implemented in this comparison.

The lattice, atomic positions, valence count, spin, pseudopotential coefficients, LDA_X plus LDA_C_VWN, fractional k points and weights are aligned. Plane-wave cutoff and SCF convergence are checked on the DFTK side. Gaussian and plane-wave calculations use different finite spaces, so machine-precision agreement is not demanded between their finite-basis energies. Agreement is assessed against the published acceptance width alongside Gaussian-basis and auxiliary-grid sensitivities and reference-cutoff dependence. Meeting this width establishes neither a rigorous bound on true error nor chemical accuracy.

Ordinary reproduction against the saved reference and reference regeneration in Julia are separate operations. Input, reference and source hashes and dependency versions are fixed, and execution from an independently extracted ZIP is checked. The release exposes numerical differences, acceptance criteria and convergence sequences as well as the result JSON’s pass flag.

Sources: Qiming Sun et al. (2020), M. F. Herbst, A. Levitt and E. Cancès (2021), Libxc developers (2026)

First-principles MD: Born–Oppenheimer and Car–Parrinello methods

First-principles molecular dynamics (AIMD) moves nuclei using electronic-structure calculations. Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics (BOMD) converges the electronic ground state at each nuclear configuration, then integrates classical nuclear motion using forces on that energy surface. E_BO below includes ionic interactions. The 1927 Born–Oppenheimer paper is cited for electronic–nuclear separation, not as the publication of a modern BOMD program.

In BOMD, SCF tolerances must control forces and trajectory reproducibility as well as energies. Atom-centered finite Gaussian bases require force contributions from basis-position dependence (Pulay terms). Finite-difference force checks, timestep refinement and energy drift in unthermostatted NVE trajectories are separate tests. Predicting an electronic initial guess does not remove the requirement to optimize each configuration to adequate accuracy.

Car–Parrinello molecular dynamics (CPMD) propagates nuclear coordinates and electronic orbitals together through an extended Lagrangian. The fictitious orbital mass μ is a numerical parameter, rather than the physical electron mass. Lagrange multipliers Λ enforce orthonormality. The displayed convention uses a μ/2 orbital-velocity term at fixed cell and occupations. Generalization to periodic k sampling must consistently include weights and occupations in electronic terms.

CPMD orbital propagation does not represent real electronic excitations as in TDDFT. Electronic fictitious motion must remain separated in timescale from nuclear motion, keeping orbitals near the BO surface. Vary μ, timestep and orthogonality tolerance while monitoring fictitious kinetic energy and energy transfer to nuclei. Distinguish the ideal unthermostatted extended-system conserved energy E_ext from nuclear kinetic plus BO energy. These statements do not establish applicability to narrow-gap systems or metals.

This section is reading only. This chapter’s fixed one-atom He example validates static total energies and k-point, basis, auxiliary-grid and SCF convergence. Multiatom He forces, energy finite differences, an independent reference and the BOMD force interface are covered in the separate From DFT to atomic forces chapter and release. Long BOMD/CPMD trajectories, timestep/SCF/fictitious-mass sensitivity and thermostats require separate validation.

Download and verify the results

Install dependencies in the extracted edition directory and use its fixed input. Choose a new or empty output directory. The ordinary runner compares with the saved DFTK reference. Regenerating that reference in Julia is a separate operation with its own packaged environment and instructions.

Primary publications, supporting sources and review scope

Bibliographic, abstract, selected full-text and official API checks are distinguished below. They do not claim reproduction or audit of an entire paper. Full papers and third-party source code are not reprinted in this tutorial.

  1. Felix Bloch (1929). Über die Quantenmechanik der Elektronen in Kristallgittern. Zeitschrift für Physik 52, 555–600

    Publisher bibliography and abstract consulted, distinguishing receipt in 1928 from publication in 1929. No full-paper reproduction or audit claimed.

  2. P. Hohenberg and W. Kohn (1964). Inhomogeneous Electron Gas. Physical Review 136, B864–B871

    Original bibliography and DOI checked against the existing Atlas. Cited for the theoretical foundation, not as a proof of the theorem by this finite-basis calculation.

    Original bibliography and DOI checked against the existing Atlas. Cited as the Kohn–Sham source without claiming numerical reproduction of the entire paper.

    Original bibliography and DOI checked against the existing Atlas. The example’s Γ-containing mesh convention is specified in the text/input rather than equated with every mesh in the paper.

  5. S. H. Vosko, L. Wilk and M. Nusair (1980). Accurate spin-dependent electron liquid correlation energies for local spin density calculations: a critical analysis. Canadian Journal of Physics 58, 1200–1211

    Original DOI and bibliography checked through official Libxc documentation identifying LDA_C_VWN as VWN5. Publisher text was inaccessible; no full-text or table audit was performed.

  6. S. Goedecker, M. Teter and J. Hutter (1996). Separable dual-space Gaussian pseudopotentials. Physical Review B 54, 1703–1710

    Publisher bibliography and abstract consulted. Actual He coefficients are aligned through the packaged data and libraries, not presented as a full-precision transcription from the paper’s tables.

bratu-inverse.title: Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients
bratu-inverse.html:
Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients

A forward problem computes a state from a coefficient; an inverse problem estimates that coefficient from observations of the state. Fit one Bratu parameter λ to five observations and use the previous chapter’s discrete adjoint gradient in the actual optimization updates. The model, boundary conditions and observation positions are known in this small synthetic problem.

Specify the known inputs and the unknown parameter

State u, coordinate x and coefficient λ are dimensionless in this educational model. The grid, interval [0,1], zero Dirichlet boundary conditions, observation operator H and weights W are fixed. Only λ is unknown; model form and boundary values are not inferred simultaneously. Use centered differences with n interior unknowns and re-solve the nonlinear equation at each trial parameter.

Observation operators and weighted least squares

Five sensors lie at x=0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.875. They coincide with grid nodes for n=15,31,63,127, so H selects interior state entries; no interpolation error is introduced. A row observing a fixed zero endpoint is zero. Save the observations d before optimization and keep them fixed rather than regenerating them for each trial λ.

All published experiments use γ=0 and wⱼ=1/5, making the objective half the mean squared observation residual. The implementation also accepts positive nonuniform weights and γ≥0, with separate tests for the weights and explicit prior term. Interpreting W as an inverse error covariance would require a specified probability model; none is assumed here.

Build an adjoint gradient from observation residuals

The state partial derivative q includes both the transpose of H and the observation weights. With the Lagrangian convention Φ−pᵀF, subtract pᵀF_λ from the explicit parameter derivative. Since F_λ=−exp(u), the Bratu state-mediated term has a plus sign. Setting γ=0 removes the explicit term, not the state-mediated term.

Assemble J at the converged primal state and solve Jᵀp=q using the existing implicit-differentiation linear algebra. Do not differentiate an unrolled Newton iteration sequence. This Bratu J is symmetric: an independent nonsymmetric manufactured problem tests transposition in the previous release, while the new dedicated tests check the observation operator, nonuniform weights and regularization.

There is one parameter and one objective, so a direct sensitivity solve Js=exp(u) also has one right-hand side. This example demonstrates no adjoint speed advantage. It checks a construction that can extend to many parameters on a small inverse problem.

Run a gradient method with box constraints

Update λ using its current adjoint gradient g and project into the interval. Restart the step length at a=10 on each iteration and halve it until the sufficient-decrease inequality holds. Use the actual displacement after projection in gΔλ. Accepted and rejected trial evaluations use the same primal controls. A failed state solve stops the calculation rather than supplying a valid objective value.

G(λ)=λ−Π[ℓ,b](λ−g(λ)),∣G(λ)∣≤10−10.G(\lambda)=\lambda-\Pi_{[\ell,b]}(\lambda-g(\lambda)),\qquad |G(\lambda)|\le10^{-10}.G(λ)=λ−Π[ℓ,b]​(λ−g(λ)),∣G(λ)∣≤10−10.

The stopping measure is the absolute projected-gradient mapping with a unit step. It equals the ordinary gradient at an interior solution where projection is inactive; at an active bound a nonzero g can satisfy constrained stationarity. Save every accepted point, step length, backtrack count, primal/adjoint residual and termination reason, with at most 300 updates and 50 line-search trials. A small objective change alone is not the convergence test.

Armijo (1966) provides the sufficient-decrease and variable-step idea; this implementation applies it to the projected displacement. The original unconstrained convergence theorem is not cited as a global-convergence guarantee for this nonlinear inverse problem. This is also not an implementation of BFGS or a general constrained-optimization library.

Keep three synthetic data regimes distinct

ddisc=Hhuh(λ∗),djcont=uα∗(xj),dnoisy=dcont+10−3(1,−0.6,0.4,−1,0.3)T.d^{\rm disc}=H_hu_h(\lambda_*),\qquad d^{\rm cont}_j=u_{\alpha_*}(x_j),\qquad d^{\rm noisy}=d^{\rm cont}+10^{-3}(1,-0.6,0.4,-1,0.3)^T.ddisc=Hh​uh​(λ∗​),djcont​=uα∗​​(xj​),dnoisy=dcont+10−3(1,−0.6,0.4,−1,0.3)T.
  1. Noiseless data from the same discretization. Generate d with the n=31 forward solver and invert with that same discretization. Recovering λ* is an inverse crime: it checks consistency among data generation, observations, gradient and optimizer, not accuracy for the continuous problem or real measurements.
  2. Noiseless data from the independent continuous family. Fix the closed-form u_α values at the observation points. Refine the inverse grid through n=15,31,63,127 to examine discretization bias in the difference from the generating parameter.
  3. Data with a fixed perturbation. Add the displayed deterministic vector once to the same continuous observations. No random draw or known noise distribution is assumed, and no resampling occurs. The published perturbed-data fit uses n=63. A best fit displaced from λ* need not indicate optimizer failure.

Verification: gradients, optimization, grids and observations

The saved measurements and input data record figure values, controls, residuals and termination reasons.

gFD(ε)=Φh(λ+ε)−Φh(λ−ε)2ε,Fh(uh(λ±ε),λ±ε)=0.g_{\rm FD}(\varepsilon)=\frac{\Phi_h(\lambda+\varepsilon)-\Phi_h(\lambda-\varepsilon)}{2\varepsilon},\qquad F_h(u_h(\lambda\pm\varepsilon),\lambda\pm\varepsilon)=0.gFD​(ε)=2εΦh​(λ+ε)−Φh​(λ−ε)​,Fh​(uh​(λ±ε),λ±ε)=0.
  1. Check gradients away from stationary points. Re-solve the state at λ±ε for several λ and compare objective-only central differences with adjoint gradients. Do not rely only on both gradients being nearly zero at an optimum.
  2. Use an independent scalar reference. Compare the adjoint-gradient fit with objective-only golden-section search. Golden section assumes a unimodal objective; sampled objective landscapes are also saved. Agreement is not a proof of global optimality across all branches.
  3. Use three starting values. Compare accepted updates, objective decrease, projected gradients and termination reasons from 0.5,1.5,3.2.
  4. Vary the data generation and grid separately. Record same-discretization consistency, mesh error for continuous data and the shift in best fit under the fixed perturbation.

Saved measurements 1: gradient checks. At n=31 and λ=0.8,1.8,3.0, central differences with ε=10⁻⁵ differ from adjoint gradients by approximately 1.31×10⁻¹², 2.81×10⁻¹² and 1.79×10⁻¹². The maximum absolute direct-sensitivity/adjoint gradient difference is below 1.4×10⁻¹⁷. The JSON also saves a perturbation sweep. These check derivatives of the implemented discrete objective.

Measurements 2: same-discretization recovery. For n=31, starts λ=0.5,1.5,3.2 take 33,30,25 accepted updates. Absolute errors from λ* are approximately 1.48×10⁻⁹, 1.10×10⁻⁹ and 1.65×10⁻⁹. All three projected gradients are at most 10⁻¹⁰ and data RMS residuals below 3.9×10⁻¹⁰. Read this close agreement as a same-discretization consistency check.

Measurements 3: mesh dependence for continuous data. For n=15,31,63,127, fitted λ values are approximately 2.6816989071, 2.6839024768, 2.6844527616, 2.6845902950. Absolute errors from λ* are approximately 2.9372×10⁻³, 7.3366×10⁻⁴, 1.8338×10⁻⁴, 4.5842×10⁻⁵, decreasing by about four as h halves. Observed orders are 2.0013, 2.0003, 2.0001. The optimizer converges while finite-mesh bias remains.

Measurements 4: a fixed perturbation shifts the best fit. At n=63 the fitted λ≈2.6841620622 shifts by about −2.9070×10⁻⁴ from the unperturbed optimum on the same grid. Absolute error from λ* is about 4.7408×10⁻⁴, data RMS residual about 7.1942×10⁻⁴ and objective about 2.5878×10⁻⁷. The projected gradient is about 6.39×10⁻¹¹, so the departure from truth is not explained simply by unfinished optimization.

The four continuous-data fits and the fixed-perturbation fit agree with the objective-only golden-section reference to within 2.1×10⁻⁹ in λ. The reference’s final interval width is below about 8.65×10⁻⁹; it is not a certificate of an exact optimum. Primal residuals at the eight final fits above are at most 1.4×10⁻¹¹. Judge derivative agreement, optimizer stopping and closeness to the generating parameter separately.

Observations that can and cannot identify λ

Js=eu,d(Hhuh)dλ=Hhs,∥W1/2Hhs∥2>0 is a local sensitivity diagnostic.J s=e^u,\qquad \frac{d(H_hu_h)}{d\lambda}=H_hs,\qquad \|W^{1/2}H_hs\|_2>0\ \text{is a local sensitivity diagnostic}.Js=eu,dλd(Hh​uh​)​=Hh​s,∥W1/2Hh​s∥2​>0 is a local sensitivity diagnostic.

A response of the interior observations to λ is a useful local sensitivity diagnostic in this scalar problem. A weak response can amplify small data changes into large parameter changes. Local sensitivity alone does not prove global uniqueness. Changing the branch, sensor positions or admissible interval changes the inverse problem.

For a counterexample, observe only x=0,1. Their fixed Dirichlet values vanish independently of λ, so H=0 and Hs=0. With γ=0, the objective is independent of λ and the data cannot identify it. Dedicated tests check this property, and the fitting function rejects this setting as uninformative. A regularization term could select a parameter but would not make the boundary observations informative.

The fixed-perturbation experiment supplies no statistical confidence intervals. Real observations, unknown model discrepancy, optimal sensor placement and identifiability of many parameters are outside the verified scope.

Separate parameter error from optimization error

Error from the generating λ*, observation residual, primal residual, adjoint residual and projected gradient are different quantities. A small projected gradient checks stationarity for the chosen grid, observations and constraints; it does not guarantee truth recovery or a zero observation residual. Conversely, continuous/discrete mismatch or fixed observation perturbations can move a well-converged optimum away from λ*.

Primal solves use an unscaled Euclidean residual tolerance of 10⁻¹⁰ and at most 40 updates. Adjoint systems use small dense matrices. Finite-difference gradient checks balance perturbation truncation, roundoff and inner-solve error. Mesh refinement, tighter optimizer stopping and improvement of a physical model address different errors.

This release is an educational scalar, box-constrained fit on a specified Bratu branch. It is not a general inverse-problem library, quasi-Newton implementation, transient adjoint, singular-point continuation method, model-selection procedure or validation of a physical model with experimental data.

Run the fixed release and inspect its inputs

Extract the dated release ZIP and follow the README. The earlier AD and sensitivity supplements remain separate, fixed releases; this synthetic inverse example has its own package.

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python scripts/build_bratu_inverse.py
python -m pytest tests/test_bratu_inverse.py

Inspect the objective, adjoint and optimizer source, figure and evidence builder, dedicated tests, independent-extraction verification record and file inventory and SHA-256 hashes. JSON inputs include positions, generating parameter, fixed perturbation, weights, starts and stopping controls.

Blondel et al. (2022), Section 2.1, and the official JAXopt documentation discuss root derivatives built from residual derivatives and linear solves; Jameson (1988) gives historical context for adjoints in design. This NumPy educational implementation does not claim to reproduce their paper experiments or JAXopt’s implementation or performance.

Implicit differentiation and Bratu sensitivity · Automatic differentiation foundation · General gradient and quasi-Newton reading

Next: two-coefficient Bratu fitting, regularization and identifiability — This chapter retains its dated supplement’s scope; the multi-parameter extension has a separate chapter and release.

Publication scope and related entries

An educational box-constrained adjoint-gradient implementation estimates one Bratu coefficient λ from synthetic observations. Measured checks cover same-discretization consistency, mesh dependence for independent continuous-family data, fixed observation perturbations, gradient differences and an objective-only reference search. Scope is a specified smaller-solution branch, fixed observations and small dense matrices. It does not validate BFGS or optimization methods generally, all-branch uniqueness, real data, statistical uncertainty or unknown model discrepancy.

  • Gradient and quasi-Newton optimization
  • Implicit differentiation and adjoint methods
  • Automatic differentiation
  • Armijo-damped Newton

periodic-forces.title: From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface
periodic-forces.html:
From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface

Atomic forces are obtained as position derivatives of the total energy in a multiatom periodic He cell. Analytic gradients, finite differences of energies and an independent plane-wave calculation are compared, separating orbital-basis, k-point, auxiliary-grid and SCF effects on forces. The requirements for a BOMD force interface are distinguished from the additional validation of trajectories.

This educational verification uses a fixed cell, a local He GTH potential and spin-unpolarized LDA. It is an execution and validation driver using PySCF analytic nuclear gradients, rather than a new electronic-structure engine. Agreement for this configuration does not validate other elements, nonlocal pseudopotentials, stress, long BOMD trajectories or thermostats.

Fixed input, code, tests and acceptance · Periodic DFT foundations · Cross-field path · ZIP · Independent-extraction verification / JSON

Forces are negative gradients of the total energy

For a fixed lattice, electron count, functional and pseudopotential, the electronic ground state is solved at each atomic configuration. The Born–Oppenheimer energy is the total cell energy, including electronic and periodic ion–ion terms. The force on Cartesian component α of atom I is minus the total derivative with respect to that coordinate. Gradient and force signs must be distinguished: coordinates in bohr and energies in hartree give forces in hartree/bohr.

The input is a cubic cell of side 5 bohr with He positions (0.37, 0.61, 0.83) and (2.13, 2.27, 2.41) bohr: four valence electrons in a closed-shell fixed configuration. It avoids a check in which symmetry makes every force zero. Directions and all x, y and z components are compared, as well as magnitudes. Numerical agreement for this artificial arrangement does not predict an equilibrium helium crystal or establish chemical accuracy. Stress and pressure require cell derivatives, separate from atomic-position derivatives at fixed cell.

The Hellmann–Feynman theorem and Pulay terms from moving bases

For a normalized exact eigenstate, the energy derivative with respect to a parameter equals the expectation of the Hamiltonian derivative. This is the Hellmann–Feynman relation. Feynman’s 1939 paper is a historical primary source for evaluating molecular forces directly. The theorem alone does not make every force correct for an electronic state represented in a finite atom-centered basis. The H and Ψ below express the general theorem; they do not replace the Kohn–Sham total energy by a sum of orbital eigenvalues.

A Gaussian basis moving with the atoms changes its functions and overlap matrix when nuclei move. Even with variationally optimized orbital coefficients, derivatives of this basis dependence must be included when differentiating the discrete energy. These are Pulay terms. The overlap derivative contracted with an energy-weighted density in the generalized eigenproblem is one contribution. The driver uses PySCF analytic nuclear gradients; it does not substitute a bare electron–ion Coulomb force.

At fixed cell and cutoff, plane waves do not move with atomic positions. Finite-cutoff force errors nevertheless remain, and SCF and density-grid errors must still be controlled. The absence of moving-atom basis terms does not make plane-wave forces exact. Basis changes under cell deformation and Pulay stress are distinct from this fixed-cell test.

Finite-difference checks: smaller displacements are not always better

One Cartesian component of one atom is displaced by ±h from the baseline configuration. At each displaced geometry the SCF is converged independently, and the resulting total energies give a central-difference force. The lattice, k points and weights, basis name, FFT grid, functional, pseudopotential and electron count are aligned. The atom-centered basis moves too, so this probes derivatives of the same discrete energy including basis-position dependence.

For a smooth energy surface, central-difference truncation is O(h²). SCF solution and roundoff errors in energies are divided by 2h, so very small displacements can increase errors. Several h values are retained to locate a stable agreement range with analytic forces. A clean U-shaped measured curve is not assumed. An input SCF energy tolerance is not interpreted as a rigorous bound on the error of each energy.

Agreement with finite differences from the same engine checks internal consistency, including signs, components and basis derivatives. Both use shared functional and pseudopotential implementations, so this alone is not an independent physical reference. A separate plane-wave DFTK implementation provides the independent comparison here.

Sources: P. Pulay (1969), PySCF developers (2026)

Converge basis, k points, auxiliary grids and SCF for forces separately

A small energy change alone does not establish converged forces. The Gaussian orbital basis, Brillouin-zone mesh, auxiliary FFT grid and SCF stopping conditions are varied one at a time, comparing forces on the same atoms and Cartesian components. Atom ordering and axes are fixed. Summaries use an L∞-type maximum absolute component norm, distinct from a per-atom vector magnitude or a component average.

Increasing a basis’s zeta label does not necessarily produce nested spaces or monotonic force changes. Nor are all k meshes nested. The final pair of settings is compared with a published target, without presenting the increment as a rigorous complete-basis or infinite-k-point error bound. The auxiliary FFT representation of density and local potentials is a separate convergence axis from the Gaussian orbital space.

Incomplete SCF convergence also affects forces. Alongside termination flags and iteration counts, inspect stored electron-count, orbital and SCF residual diagnostics. Force sensitivity to tighter stopping conditions is measured directly, and an unconverged electronic state must not be returned to BOMD as an accepted force.

Each sweep varies one control while holding the other controls at the finite settings specified in the public input. Basis sequences are checked separately at Γ and 2³, but no joint calculation combines 4³ sampling, the largest Gaussian basis and the finest FFT grid. Independent-reference agreement applies only to the designated Γ and 2³ cases.

Independent reference: the same model in a different discretization

PySCF uses a periodic Gaussian basis and FFTDF; the reference uses DFTK’s plane-wave Hamiltonian, SCF, periodic ion interactions and analytic forces. Lattice and all atomic positions, valence count, spin restriction and integer occupations, every local-GTH coefficient, Libxc LDA_X plus LDA_C_VWN (VWN5), fractional k points and weights are matched. No fitted energy offset or force correction is applied.

The DFTK plane-wave cutoff is increased separately and its final force increment is measured. This is not a rounding-error comparison of identical finite matrices. Different finite Gaussian and plane-wave spaces are assessed using the published acceptance width and convergence diagnostics on both sides. Both engines share Libxc, which limits the extent of implementation independence.

DFTK compute_forces returns a representation associated with fractional coordinates; the Cartesian API is compute_forces_cart. Coordinate and force transformations are different. Comparisons here use Cartesian components in hartree/bohr throughout. The generation script, pinned Julia environment, pseudopotential, input and result hashes are retained. Comparing against the saved reference in Python and regenerating the reference in Julia are distinct operations.

Check components, translation and nonzero forces

A configuration with nearly zero forces can pass even with a sign error. A multiatom configuration carrying nonzero forces is used, with componentwise comparisons of analytic forces, finite differences and the independent reference. A single force norm should not hide component permutations, atom-order mistakes or incorrect units.

In an ideal periodic system without external fields, uniform translation leaves the total energy unchanged and the sum of atomic forces vanishes. Finite real-space grids can numerically break this property; the remaining total force is a useful grid and differentiation diagnostic. Translation checks alone do not establish accurate relative forces, so energy differences and an independent reference are used alongside them.

Sources: DFTK developers (2026), PySCF developers (2026)

The BOMD interface and additional trajectory validation

The BOMD force provider energy_and_forces accepts positions_bohr and returns energy_per_cell and forces_cartesian from the same energy surface, together with SCF convergence and residual diagnostics. An unconverged electronic state is treated as a failure. Masses belong to nuclear time integration, not as factors multiplying the DFT potential energy or forces. Wrapped positions inside a periodic cell must be distinguished from a continuous trajectory record.

Velocity Verlet advances velocities by half a step, updates positions, solves the electronic problem again for the new forces, then completes the velocity update. Carrying an electronic guess from a previous step accelerates the calculation but does not replace SCF convergence. This verification focuses on atomic forces and the BOMD handoff; a single force evaluation or short interface smoke test is not counted as validation of long trajectories.

Accepting a practical trajectory additionally requires timestep refinement, tighter-SCF comparisons, total-energy and momentum checks in unthermostatted NVE, and time-reversal checks where appropriate. Thermostats can hide force or integration errors by absorbing energy changes, so unthermostatted checks come first. Small short-time drift does not guarantee long-time stability or a correct statistical distribution.

Car–Parrinello dynamics is a distinct formulation propagating fictitious electronic degrees of freedom alongside nuclei. A force provider on the Born–Oppenheimer surface is not a CPMD implementation. The cross-field navigation separately shows the executed scope of DFT, force evaluation, nuclear integration and temperature control.

Install dependencies in the extracted edition directory and use its fixed input. Choose a new or empty output directory. The ordinary runner compares with the saved DFTK reference. Regenerating that reference in Julia is a separate operation with its own packaged environment and instructions.

Primary publications, supporting sources and review scope

Bibliographic, abstract, selected full-text and official API checks are distinguished below. They do not claim reproduction or audit of an entire paper. Full papers and third-party source code are not reprinted in this tutorial.

    Publisher bibliography and abstract consulted. Actual He coefficients are aligned through the packaged data and libraries, not presented as a full-precision transcription from the paper’s tables.

  2. S. H. Vosko, L. Wilk and M. Nusair (1980). Accurate spin-dependent electron liquid correlation energies for local spin density calculations: a critical analysis. Canadian Journal of Physics 58, 1200–1211

    Original DOI and bibliography checked through official Libxc documentation identifying LDA_C_VWN as VWN5. Publisher text was inaccessible; no full-text or table audit was performed.

  3. Qiming Sun et al. (2020). Recent developments in the PySCF program package. The Journal of Chemical Physics 153, 024109

    Publisher bibliography/abstract and the existing Atlas entry consulted. The periodic APIs used here are additionally checked against official documentation and pinned code.

  4. M. F. Herbst, A. Levitt and E. Cancès (2021). DFTK: A Julian approach for simulating electrons in solids. Proceedings of the JuliaCon Conferences 3(26), 69

    Publisher bibliography and the introduction of the open paper consulted. The reference calculation is a separate numerical check, not a reproduction of all paper examples.

  5. DFTK developers (2026). DFTK API and pseudopotentials. Official DFTK documentation

    Selected API descriptions of compute_forces, compute_forces_cart, coordinates, units and derivatives of discrete energies consulted. Reference generation uses the packaged pinned DFTK environment, whose source is also checked.

  6. M. Born and R. Oppenheimer (1927). Zur Quantentheorie der Molekeln. Annalen der Physik 389(20), 457–484

    Publisher bibliography and DOI checked. Cited for the historical basis of Born–Oppenheimer separation, without claiming a full-text audit or reproduction of a modern MD implementation.

    Publisher bibliography/abstract and original equations (3)–(5) and discussion of fictitious electronic motion near the BO surface consulted. The paper’s silicon dynamics have not been numerically reproduced.

  8. R. P. Feynman (1939). Forces in Molecules. Physical Review 56, 340–343

    Publisher bibliography and abstract consulted. Cited as a historical primary source for the Hellmann–Feynman force relation, not as sole validation of finite-basis or pseudopotential gradient implementations.

Multi-parameter Bratu inversion: regularization and identifiability

Adding a second coefficient changes what a successful fit can tell us. Observations may respond strongly to one parameter combination and barely change along another. We extend the previous constant λ to a spatial coefficient λ(x), separating adjoint-gradient fitting, selection by regularization and information supplied by observations.

Extend constant λ to a level and a slope

The unknown a sets the coefficient level and b multiplies the tilt basis (2x−1). The actual spatial derivative dλ/dx and the end-to-end difference λ(1)−λ(0) both equal 2b. Setting b=0 recovers the constant-coefficient Bratu model. This is a two-basis-function extension of the coefficient, rather than duplicate estimates of one constant λ. State, coordinate and both parameters are dimensionless. Domain, mesh, zero Dirichlet data and observation operator are fixed.

The published experiments use the box and generating vector θ*=(2.2,0.35) above. A positive coefficient does not imply identifiability. These bounds alone do not guarantee existence, uniqueness or convergence for arbitrary meshes and starting states. Every primal solve starts at zero and uses damped Newton with an explicit residual acceptance check; the tested smaller-solution branch defines the scope.

Fix the observations and their numerical generator

The ordinary experiment samples x=0.125,0.25,0.5,0.75,0.875. All are exact interior nodes on the inverse meshes, so H selects state components. Observations at mirrored locations are retained separately: symmetric sensor positions do not discard the left-right difference. The published weights are wⱼ=1/5. They weight observations, rather than approximate a spatial integral.

A noiseless control generated and fitted on the same mesh first checks recovery of both coefficients. It is an inverse crime used for code consistency. Separate fixed observations from a numerical reference, with its own refinement check, support inverse-mesh refinement. For b≠0 we do not reuse the closed-form constant-coefficient Bratu family as an analytic reference. The saved inputs and evidence specify the actual generator, resolution and self-refinement difference.

The numerical generator uses a separate Newton implementation with Thomas elimination for tridiagonal systems. Grids n=255,511,1023 are compared, and n=1023 observations are fixed. Linear-system implementations differ, but both use second-order centered finite differences. The finer grid is not an exact continuous solution, and parameter error also contains its finite-grid error. Generator controls use the infinity norm of h²F and final Newton correction, recorded separately from the unscaled inverse-solve residual.

A perturbed experiment likewise saves the observations once, before fitting. Trials do not regenerate data, and different γ values use the same perturbation. Noise here means a deterministic observation perturbation; no probability distribution or real measurement is assumed.

Obtain both gradient components from one adjoint equation

Assume a smooth selected state branch and a locally nonsingular state Jacobian J. Invertibility of the primal Jacobian J and full column rank of the observation Jacobian Adata are separate conditions. With the Lagrangian convention Φ−pᵀF, the residual parameter derivative Bθ has two columns, while p has one right-hand side. The state partial q includes Hᵀ and W. Multiplication by Bθᵀp produces both components of g. The state-mediated term Qᵀ(exp(u)⊙p) remains when γ=0. We differentiate the converged discrete equation, rather than unroll a finite sequence of Newton iterations.

The direct sensitivity S uses two right-hand sides. It provides an independent gradient diagnostic. Actual optimization directions use the adjoint gradient; neither finite differences nor direct sensitivities substitute for it. A two-parameter example with small dense matrices does not establish an unmeasured speed advantage.

Vary regularization and inspect prior bias

The Tikhonov-type quadratic penalty adds distance from θprior to the observation misfit. The implementation uses Euclidean distance, equivalent to the regularization matrix R=I₂. Zero, weak and stronger penalties are applied to identical observations, recording data residual, distance from the prior and error against the generating vector separately. Increasing γ need not move the estimate closer to the generating truth.

A displaced prior pulls the estimate toward its own values. Regularization may suppress amplification of observation perturbations along a weak direction while introducing prior bias. A synthetic experiment can compare parameter errors because θ* is known; this does not supply a corresponding choice rule for real data. The published γ sweep illustrates sensitivity and bias. It does not validate automatic tuning, cross-validation, an L-curve corner rule or statistical confidence intervals.

Hansen’s author-maintained manual describes the quadratic penalty, augmented least squares and spectral analysis. Its squared regularization parameter corresponds to γ here. Its linear formulas are distinguished from this implemented nonlinear coefficient fit.

Optimize with a fixed scaling of the adjoint gradient

P=diag(1,100) is a fixed positive diagonal matrix that adjusts progress along the differently sensitive level and slope directions. The evidence records P, initial step, halving rule, Armijo constant, iteration limits and tolerances. P adds no observation and is not a Gauss–Newton matrix estimated from the data. Rescaling an optimizer is distinct from improving identifiability.

The Armijo inner product uses the actual projected displacement Δθ. Stopping uses the unit-step projected gradient G without P, so a small preconditioned update alone cannot imply convergence. A bound-constrained stationary point may have nonzero gradient components at active bounds. At most 1000 updates and 50 backtracking trials are allowed. Inspect the termination reason and accepted history; closeness to the generating vector is not a stopping criterion.

Diagnose data-only sensitivity with singular values

The right singular vector v₂ associated with a small σ₂ identifies a coefficient combination with little effect on those observations. Two independent observed directions yield full column rank at this point. This is a local diagnostic for the chosen state branch and observation operator, rather than a proof of global uniqueness for the nonlinear inverse problem.

Singular values and condition numbers depend on observation weights, parameter units and parameter scaling. The published SVD uses T=I₂, the raw (a,b) coordinates. Changes of units or coefficient basis require the scaling to be stated. Numerical rank counts singular values above 10⁻¹⁰σ₁ and records that absolute threshold as well. A small singular value is not a universal identification threshold independent of measurement precision and floating-point error.
